Segnosaurus.etymology: From Latin 'segnis' meaning 'slow' and Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'; meaning 'slow lizard.' The specific name galbinensis refers to the Galbin region of the Gobi Desert.
Segnosaurus.description: Segnosaurus is a genus of therizinosaurid dinosaur that lived in what is now southeastern Mongolia during the Late Cretaceous, about 102-86 million years ago. Multiple incomplete but well-preserved specimens were discovered in the Gobi Desert in the 1970s, and in 1979 the genus and species Segnosaurus galbinensis were named. The generic name Segnosaurus means "slow lizard" and the specific name galbinensis refers to the Galbin region. The known material of this dinosaur includes the lower jaw, neck and tail vertebrae, the pelvis, shoulder girdle, and limb bones. Parts of the specimens have gone missing or become damaged since they were collected. Remains from Japan originally assigned to Allosaurus were reassigned to Segnosaurus sp. (of unspecified species) in 2025.

Sektensaurus.etymology: From Tehuelche sekten, meaning "island", combined with Greek sauros, "lizard" - means "island lizard"
Sektensaurus.description: Sektensaurus is a genus of ornithopod dinosaur, possibly an elasmarian, from the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian) of Patagonia, Argentina. Its remains were uncovered in the fluvial tuffs of the Lago Colhué Huapí Formation in the Golfo San Jorge Basin. The type and only species is S. sanjuanboscoi. Sektensaurus is the first non-hadrosauroid ornithopod of central Patagonia. The discovery of the genus increases the anatomical knowledge of ornithopods and adds new data on the compositions of dinosaur faunas that lived in Patagonia close to Antarctica at the end of the Cretaceous.

Shantungosaurus.etymology: Named after Shandong (historically romanised as Shantung) Province in China, where fossils were found, combined with Greek 'sauros' (lizard), meaning 'Shandong lizard'.
Shantungosaurus.description: Shantungosaurus is an extinct genus of very large herbivorous saurolophine hadrosaurid dinosaur found in the Late Cretaceous Wangshi Group of the Shandong Peninsula in China, containing a single species, Shantungosaurus giganteus. The stratigraphic interval of Shantungosaurus ranges from the top of the Xingezhuang Formation to the middle of the Hongtuya Formation, middle to late Campanian in age. Shantungosaurus is so far the largest hadrosauroid taxon in the world, with size estimates around 15-17 meters (49-56 ft) in length and 13-16 metric tons (14-18 short tons) in body mass.

Ischium straight and long with extremely weak, small apical expansion at terminal end
Exceptionally large body size with total assembled length exceeding the known Hadrosaurinae

Shanyangosaurus.etymology: Named after the Shanyang Formation (Shanyang County, Shaanxi, China) where it was found, combined with Greek sauros, "lizard" - means "Shanyang lizard"
Shanyangosaurus.description: Shanyangosaurus is a genus of theropod dinosaur found in Shaanxi, China, and known only from a partial sacrum, partial scapula, humeri, femur, tibia, metatarsals, and phalanges found in the Maastrichtian aged Shanyang Formation. The bones are reportedly hollow; this, along with other features of the femur and known foot bones, suggest it is a member of the coelurosauria, but a specific family cannot be determined without more material. Holtz et al. assigned Shanyangosaurus to Avetheropoda.

Shaochilong.etymology: From Chinese '鲨齿' (shāchǐ) meaning 'shark tooth' and '龙' (lóng) meaning 'dragon'; meaning 'shark-toothed dragon', referring to its shark-like serrated teeth.
Shaochilong.description: Shaochilong is an extinct genus of tetanuran theropod dinosaurs from the Early Cretaceous (Barremian to Albian stages) Miaogou Formation of China, though a more restrictive suggestion from the Aptian to the Albian has been suggested based on faunal composition. It was usually described as a carcharodontosaurid, but other phylogenies have suggested a different position as a tyrannosauroid or as a member of polytomic allosauroid. The genus contains a single species, Shaochilong maortuensis, which was originally placed in the genus Chilantaisaurus as C. maortuensis, but was re-described and reclassified in 2009.

Shenzhousaurus.etymology: Named after Shenzhou, a poetic name for China, combined with Greek sauros, "lizard" - means "Shenzhou lizard"
Shenzhousaurus.description: Shenzhousaurus is a genus of basal ornithomimosaurian theropod dinosaur from the Lower Cretaceous of China.The holotype (NGMC 97-4-002, National Geological Museum of China) was collected from near the bottom (fluvial beds) of the Yixian Formation (Aptian) at the Sihetun fossil site, Beipiao, western Liaoning Province. This specimen consists of a partial skeleton preserved on a sandstone slab in a "death pose," its head above the torso. The distal parts of the hindlimbs, distal portion of the tail, and the forelimbs (except for part of the right hand) and the pectoral girdle are missing. The head is crushed, exposing the left side obliquely.

Shidaisaurus.etymology: Named for the Jin-Shidai ('Golden Age') Company, which oversaw excavation and inspection of the Jurassic World Park near the discovery site, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Shidaisaurus.description: Shidaisaurus is a genus of metriacanthosaurid dinosaur. Its fossil was found in early Middle Jurassic-age rocks of the Chuanjie Formation in Yunnan, China. It is known from a partial skeleton, holotype DML-LCA 9701-IV, found at the bottom of an assemblage of nine dinosaur individuals, lacking most of the tail vertebrae, ribs, pectoral girdle, and limb bones. Shidaisaurus was described in 2009 by Wu and colleagues. The type species is Shidaisaurus jinae. Generic name and specific name in combination refer to the Jin-Shidai ("Golden Age") Company that oversaw excavation and inspection of the Jurassic World Park near the site.

Shingopana.etymology: From Swahili 'shingo' meaning 'neck' and 'pana' meaning 'wide'; meaning 'wide neck', in reference to the animal's broad neck.
Shingopana.description: Shingopana is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod from the Upper Cretaceous (late Campanian-early Maastrichtian age) Galula Formation of Tanzania. Gorscak & O'Connor's phylogenetic testing suggest Shingopana is more closely related to the South American titanosaur family of Aeolosaurini than any of the titanosaurs found so far in North and South Africa.

Shixinggia.etymology: Named for Shixing County, Guangdong, China, where the fossil was discovered.
Shixinggia.description: Shixinggia is a genus of oviraptorosaurian dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous period of Shixing County, Guangdong, China, for which it was named. While no skull was recovered, the specimen (BVP-112) is known from a fair amount of post-cranial material that shows it was a fairly derived oviraptorosaur (slightly more advanced than Nomingia), of superfamily Caenagnathoidea. Lü et al. (2003, 2005) describe it as an oviraptorid, but it could be a caenagnathid.

Shuangbaisaurus.etymology: From "Shuangbai" (Shuangbai County in Yunnan, China, where the holotype was found) and Greek "sauros" (lizard); meaning "Shuangbai lizard".
Shuangbaisaurus.description: Shuangbaisaurus is a genus of theropod dinosaur, possibly a junior synonym of Sinosaurus. It lived in the Early Jurassic of Yunnan Province, China, and is represented by a single species, S. anlongbaoensis, known from a partial skull. Like the theropods Dilophosaurus and Sinosaurus, Shuangbaisaurus bore a pair of thin, midline crests on its skull. Unusually, these crests extended backwards over the level of the eyes, which, along with the unusual orientation of the jugal bone, led the describers to name it as a new genus. However, Shuangbaisaurus also possesses a groove between its premaxilla and maxilla, a characteristic which has been used to characterize Sinosaurus as a genus. Among the two morphotypes present within the genus Sinosaurus, Shuangbaisaurus more closely resembles the morphotype that is variably treated as a distinct species, S. sinensis, in its relatively tall skull.

Shuvuuia.description: Shuvuuia is a genus of bird-like theropod dinosaur from the late Cretaceous period of Mongolia. Siamosaurus.etymology: Named for Siam, the ancient name of Thailand, where the fossils were found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'; meaning 'Siam lizard.'
Siamosaurus.description: Siamosaurus is a potentially dubious genus of spinosaurid dinosaur that lived in what is now Thailand and possibly China during the Early Cretaceous period (Barremian to Aptian) and is the first reported spinosaurid from Asia. It is confidently known only from tooth fossils; the first were found in the Sao Khua Formation, with more teeth later recovered from the younger Khok Kruat Formation. The only species Siamosaurus suteethorni, whose name honors Thai paleontologist Varavudh Suteethorn, was formally described in 1986. In 2009, four teeth from China previously attributed to a pliosaur-under the species "Sinopliosaurus" fusuiensis-were identified as those of a spinosaurid, possibly Siamosaurus. It is yet to be determined if two partial spinosaurid skeletons from Thailand and an isolated tooth from Japan also belong to Siamosaurus.

Sinocephale.etymology: From Latin 'Sinae' (China) + Greek 'kephale' (head), meaning 'Chinese head', referring to its country of origin and the distinctive domed head typical of pachycephalosaurids.
Sinocephale.description: Sinocephale is a genus of pachycephalosaurid dinosaur that lived in what is now Inner Mongolia, China, during the Cretaceous period. The genus contains a single species, Sinocephale bexelli, which was originally named as a species of the genus Troodon in 1953, and later transferred to the genus Stegoceras in 1964. After decades of being considered dubious, it was re-evaluated in 2021 and recognized as a valid taxon, being given its own genus, Sinocephale. The original holotype was lost, with modern research conducted using rediscovered plaster casts.

Sinoceratops.description: Sinoceratops is an extinct genus of ceratopsian dinosaur that lived from 77.3 to 73.5 million years ago during the latter part of the Cretaceous Period in what is now Shandong province in China. It was named in 2010 by Xu Xing et al. for three skulls from Zhucheng, China. The name of the type species Sinoceratops zhuchengensis means "Chinese horned face from Zhucheng", after the location of its discovery. Sinoceratops was a medium-sized, averagely-built, ground-dwelling, quadrupedal herbivore. It could grow up to an estimated 5 meters (16 ft) in length and weigh up to 2 tonnes (2.0 long tons; 2.2 short tons).

Sinopeltosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'sino-' (Chinese, after the Sinae) and 'peltē' (small shield) plus 'sauros' (lizard); meaning approximately 'Chinese small-shielded lizard', a replacement name for the preoccupied Sinopelta Ulansky, 2014a.
Sinopeltosaurus.description: Sinopeltosaurus is a dubious genus of extinct thyreophoran ornithischian dinosaur described by Roman Ulansky for the articulated ankle specimen FMNH CUP 2338 from the Lower Jurassic Lufeng Formation of Yunnan, China. The type and only species is S. minimus. The specimen was originally described by Irmis and Knoll (2008) as an indeterminate basal ornithischian and was later identified as a nomen dubium by Galton and Carpenter (2016), who listed it as Ornithischia indet., possibly Thyreophora indet. Ulansky's companion paper used the variant name 'Sinopelta minima' for the same animal; Galton and Carpenter (2016) acted as first revisers under the ICZN and selected Sinopeltosaurus minimus as the official combination.

Ulansky (2014b) coined Sinopeltosaurus as the replacement name in a second DINOLOGIA paper the same year. Both Ulansky (2014) papers are treated as nomina dubia by Galton and Carpenter (2016).

Sinornithosaurus.description: Sinornithosaurus is a genus of feathered dromaeosaurid dinosaur from the early Cretaceous Period (late Barremian) of the Yixian Formation in what is now China. It was the fifth non-avian feathered dinosaur genus discovered by 1999. The original specimen was collected from the Sihetun locality of western Liaoning. It was found in the Jianshangou beds of the Yixian Formation, dated to 124.5 million years ago. Additional specimens have been found in the younger Dawangzhangzi bed, dating to around 122 million years ago.

Sinosauropteryx.etymology: From Latin/Greek 'Sino-' meaning 'Chinese', Greek 'sauros' meaning 'reptile' or 'lizard', and 'pteryx' meaning 'wing'; meaning 'Chinese reptilian wing.'
Sinosauropteryx.description: Sinosauropteryx is an extinct genus of coelurosaurian theropod dinosaurs. Described in 1996, it was the first dinosaur taxon outside of Avialae (birds and their immediate relatives) to be found with evidence of feathers. It was covered with a coat of very simple filament-like feathers. Structures that indicate the color pattern have also been preserved in some of its feathers, which show that Sinosauropteryx had a countershading pattern in its body with a banded tail. The reddish brown coloration previously inferred for Sinosauropteryx is based on the melanosomes preserved in the specimen of a separate genus, Huadanosaurus. Some contention has arisen with an alternative interpretation of the filamentous impression as remains of collagen fibers, but this has not been widely accepted.
diagnostic_features: Extremely short, primitive, uniform feathers unlike later avian forms
Over 50 extremely elongated caudal vertebrae constituting 60% of body length
Forelimb extremely short (approximately two-fifths hind limb length) with short thick humerus (~20 mm)
Relatively high, blunt-rostrum skull with elliptical but not enlarged antorbital fenestra
Robust acute dentition with over 50 extremely developed teeth
Long robust hind limb with unfused proximal metatarsals and tarsals separated

Sinosaurus.etymology: From Latin Sinae, "Chinese", combined with Greek sauros, "lizard" - means "Chinese lizard"
Sinosaurus.description: Sinosaurus is an extinct genus of basal theropod dinosaur which lived during the Early Jurassic (Hettangian-Sinemurian). Fossils of the animal have been found in the Lufeng Formation, in the Yunnan Province of China. The type species, S. triassicus, was named by Chung Chieng Young in 1940. A second species, S. sinensis, was originally assigned to Dilophosaurus, but was later reassigned to Sinosaurus. Sinosaurus is morphologically similar to Dilophosaurus including the presence of a similarly shaped cranial crest, though its precise taxonomic position is uncertain, and the two genera may not be closely related.

Sinotyrannus.etymology: From Latin 'Sinae' (a classical name for the Chinese) and Greek 'tyrannos' (tyrant); meaning 'Chinese tyrant'.
Sinotyrannus.description: Sinotyrannus is an extinct genus of large proceratosaurid tyrannosauroid theropod from the Aptian (Early Cretaceous) lower Jiufotang Formation of Kazuo County, western Liaoning Province, China — part of the Jehol Biota. The single species, Sinotyrannus kazuoensis, is known from a disarticulated skeleton (KZV-001) including the anterior skull and mandibles, three articulated dorsal vertebrae, ribs, partial ilia, and manual phalanges. Originally placed within Tyrannosauroidea (and tentatively Tyrannosauridae) by Ji et al. (2009), subsequent phylogenetic analyses (Loewen et al. 2013, and others) recovered Sinotyrannus as a basal proceratosaurid. With an estimated body length of ~9-10 m, it is one of the largest known Early Cretaceous tyrannosauroids. Cau and Paterna (2025) proposed Sinotyrannus as the adult morphotype of the coeval compsognathid Huaxiagnathus, but that hypothesis is single-paper-recent and not yet a community consensus; the genus is treated as valid here.

Maxillary fenestra reaches past the rostral margin of the antorbital fossa but stays separated from its ventral margin.
Preacetabular blade of the ilium short and lacking a ventrally expanded anterior hook.

Sphaerotholus.etymology: From Greek 'sphaira' (sphere, ball) + Greek 'tholos' (dome, domed building), meaning 'spherical dome' or 'ball dome', referring to the characteristic rounded domed skull of this pachycephalosaurid.

Spicomellus.etymology: From Latin 'spica' meaning 'spike' and Latin 'mellum' meaning 'collar', referring to the spiked osteoderms fused to the rib of the holotype specimen
Spicomellus.description: Spicomellus is an extinct genus of unusual early ankylosaurian dinosaur from the El Mers III Formation (Bathonian age) of Morocco. The genus contains a single species, Spicomellus afer, representing the oldest named definitive ankylosaur. The species was initially described in 2021 based on a single rib with fused osteoderms, rendering its life appearance and relationships uncertain. In 2025, several additional bones, including osteoderms and cranial and postcranial remains, were described, revealing that it bears a unique array of spines over the body, including extremely elongated spikes around the neck and pelvis. It likely had a tail weapon, making it the oldest known ankylosaur with this structure.

Spinophorosaurus.etymology: From Latin 'spina' meaning 'spine' or 'thorn', Greek 'phoros' meaning 'bearing' or 'carrying', and Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', referring to its spine-bearing tail clubs.
Spinophorosaurus.description: Spinophorosaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur that lived in what is now Niger during the Middle Jurassic period. The first two specimens were excavated in the 2000s by German and Spanish teams under difficult conditions. The skeletons were brought to Europe and digitally replicated, making Spinophorosaurus the first sauropod to have its skeleton 3D printed, and were to be returned to Niger in the future. Together, the two specimens represented most of the skeleton of the genus, and one of the most completely known basal sauropods of its time and place. The first skeleton was made the holotype specimen of the new genus and species Spinophorosaurus nigerensis in 2009; the generic name ("spine-bearing lizard") refers to what was initially thought to be spiked osteoderms, and the specific name (Niger and -ensis) refers to where it was found. A juvenile sauropod from the same area was later assigned to the genus.

Spinosaurus.etymology: From Latin spina (spine, thorn) and Greek sauros (lizard); meaning "spine lizard", named for the conspicuously tall neural spines of the trunk vertebrae that supported a dorsal sail.
Spinosaurus.description: Spinosaurus is the type genus of Spinosauridae and one of the most distinctive Cretaceous theropods, recognized for the enormously tall neural spines of its dorsal vertebrae that supported a dorsal sail or hump. The genus was erected by Ernst Stromer in 1915 on a partial skeleton recovered in 1912 by his collector Richard Markgraf from the Bahariya beds of the Western Desert of Egypt (specimen BSP 1912 VIII 19 in the Bayerische Staatssammlung in Munich). The original type material — including the iconic mandibles and elongate-spined dorsals — was destroyed in the British bombing of Munich in April 1944, leaving only Stromer's plates and descriptions. Stromer (1934) added more material, including a smaller specimen he treated informally as "Spinosaurus B" (later partly the basis of Russell's 1996 S. maroccanus). Ibrahim et al. (2014) designated FSAC-KK 11888, a partial skeleton from the Kem Kem beds of southeastern Morocco, as the neotype of S. aegyptiacus, and proposed on the basis of pachyostotic limb bones, retracted nostrils, and reduced hindlimbs that Spinosaurus was a semi-aquatic predator capable of obligate quadrupedal locomotion on land. Subsequent work (notably Ibrahim et al. 2020 on the paddle-tail and Sereno et al. 2022 in response) has continued to debate the degree of aquatic adaptation, but the broad picture of a piscivorous, river-dwelling spinosaurid with reduced hindlimbs and dense limb bones is now widely accepted.
diagnostic_features: Dentary rami long and low-set in the middle, bearing about 15 awl-shaped teeth per ramus, with strongly heterodont positions (large 2nd-4th, small 5th-10th, larger 11th-14th).
Teeth straight to gently curved, sub-circular in cross-section, with smooth (non-serrated) anterior and posterior keels.
Fleshy nostril retracted to a posteriorly placed narial fossa on the skull, far from the snout tip.
Free dorsal vertebral centra elongate, hourglass-shaped in dorsal view, and strongly opisthocoelous, lacking a ventral keel.
Neural spines of dorsal vertebrae extraordinarily tall (up to ~8x centrum height), laterally compressed, broadened ventrally and dorsally, supporting a dorsal sail.
Anterior dorsal centra exceptionally broad and concavoconvex, creating a horizontal cervicodorsal hinge.
Long bones (femur, tibia, manual phalanges) with solid shafts lacking an open medullary cavity; bone density 30-40% greater than in other large theropods (pachyostosis).
Femur substantially shorter than tibia and hindlimb length only ~19% of body length; iliac blade reduced to roughly half the surface area of other comparably sized theropods.

Stegoceras.etymology: From Greek 'stege' (στέγη) meaning 'roof' and 'keras' (κέρας) meaning 'horn'; meaning 'horn roof', referring to the domed skull.
Stegoceras.description: Stegoceras is a genus of pachycephalosaurid (dome-headed) dinosaur that lived in what is now North America during the Late Cretaceous period, about 77.5 to 74 million years ago (mya). The first specimens from Alberta, Canada, were described in 1902, and the type species Stegoceras validum was based on these remains. The generic name means "horn roof", and the specific name means "strong". Several other species have been placed in the genus over the years, but these have since been moved to other genera or deemed junior synonyms. Currently only S. validum and S. novomexicanum, named in 2011 from fossils found in New Mexico, remain. The validity of the latter species has also been debated, and it may not even belong to the genus Stegoceras.

Stegosaurides.etymology: From 'Stegosaurus' and Greek '-ides' meaning 'resembling' or 'shaped like'; meaning 'Stegosaurus-shaped', referencing its similarity in armoring to Stegosaurus.
Stegosaurides.description: Stegosaurides is a genus of herbivorous thyreophoran (perhaps ankylosaurid or possibly stegosaurian) dinosaur. It lived during the Cretaceous. Its fossils were found in the Xinminbao Group near Heishan in Gansu Province in China. These fossils consist of fragmentary material, including dermal spine elements. The genus is occasionally misspelled as "Stegosauroides".

Stegosaurus.etymology: From Greek stegos (roof) and sauros (lizard); meaning "roof lizard", in reference to the parasagittal rows of large dermal plates that Marsh initially interpreted as forming a roof-like carapace over the back of the animal.
Stegosaurus.description: Stegosaurus is the type genus of Stegosauridae and one of the most readily recognized dinosaurs, characterized by two parasagittal rows of large, erect dermal plates running from the cervicodorsal junction to near the tail tip and by four long tail spines (the "thagomizer") at the distal end of the tail. Marsh erected the genus and the order Stegosauria in 1877 on a partial skeleton from the Morrison Formation of Colorado, originally naming S. armatus as the type species. C. W. Gilmore's 1914 monograph on USNM 4934 (Felch Quarry No. 1, Garden Park, Colorado) supplied the first detailed osteology of the genus and resolved decades of argument over the plate arrangement, demonstrating from articulated evidence that the plates of the two rows alternate rather than pair. Because Marsh's S. armatus material is too fragmentary to anchor the genus, ICZN Opinion 2320 (2013) set aside all prior type-species fixations under plenary power and designated S. stenops Marsh, 1887, with USNM 4934 as its holotype, as the new type species — the form on which most of our modern picture of the genus rests. Several previously named species (S. duplex, Diracodon laticeps) are subsumed in Stegosaurus, while the synonymies of Hesperosaurus and Wuerhosaurus proposed by Maidment et al. (2008) remain contested in subsequent literature and are not accepted here.
diagnostic_features: Skull comparatively very small with a brain cavity proportionally among the smallest of any large terrestrial vertebrate.
Sacrum with an enormously enlarged neural canal forming a chamber many times the cranial capacity, fully roofed over by bone.
Two parasagittal rows of erect, flattened, kite-shaped dermal plates extending from the cervicodorsal junction to near the tail tip; plates of opposite rows alternating rather than paired.
Tail bearing four large dermal spines arranged in two pairs near the distal end (thagomizer); roughly 20-22 dermal plates total.
Pes tetradactyl with digit IV reduced to a vestigial metatarsal; digit V absent.
Tibia distinctive in having the greatest diameter of both ends lying approximately in the same plane.
Postzygapophyses on the posterior cervical vertebrae elongate posteriorly, overhanging the back of the centrum.
Supra-acetabular process of the ilium diverging at approximately 90 degrees from the anterior process.

Stegouros.etymology: From Greek 'stegos' meaning 'roof' and 'oura' meaning 'tail'; meaning 'roofed tail', referring to the roof-like covering of osteoderms over the tail.
Stegouros.description: Stegouros is an extinct genus of ankylosaurian dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous Dorotea Formation of southern Chile. The genus contains a single species, Stegouros elengassen, known from a semi-articulated, near-complete skeleton. Stegouros is a member of the Parankylosauria, a clade of small Gondwanan armored dinosaurs. It is characterized by its small body size and distinct arrangement of fused osteoderms forming a macuahuitl-like tail weapon.

Stenonychosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'stenos' meaning 'narrow', 'onyx/onychos' meaning 'claw', and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'; meaning 'narrow claw lizard', referring to the narrow enlarged claw on the second toe.
Stenonychosaurus.description: Stenonychosaurus is a disputed genus of troodontid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta, Canada, as well as possibly the Two Medicine Formation. The type and only species, S. inequalis, was named by Charles Mortram Sternberg in 1932, based on a foot, fragments of a hand, and some caudal vertebrae from the Late Cretaceous of Alberta. S. inequalis was reassigned in 1987 by Phil Currie to the genus Troodon, which was reverted by the recognition of Stenonychosaurus as a separate genus from the possibly dubious Troodon in 2017 by Evans et al. and also later in the same year by Van der Reest and Currie.

Struthiomimus.etymology: From Greek 'stroutheios' (στρούθειος) meaning 'of the ostrich' and 'mimos' (μῖμος) meaning 'mimic' or 'imitator'; meaning 'ostrich mimic', referring to its long-legged, ostrich-like build.
Struthiomimus.description: Struthiomimus is a genus of ornithomimid dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous of what is now western North America. They were long-legged, bipedal, ostrich-like dinosaurs with toothless beaks. The type species, Struthiomimus altus, is one of the more common, smaller dinosaurs found in Dinosaur Provincial Park. Their overall abundance, in addition to their toothless beak, suggests that these animals were mainly herbivorous or (more likely) omnivorous, rather than purely carnivorous. Similar to the modern ostriches, emus, and rheas (among other birds), these dinosaurs likely lived as opportunistic omnivores, supplementing a largely plant-based diet with a variety of small mammals, reptiles, amphibians, insects, invertebrates, and anything else they could fit into their mouth, as they foraged.

Styracosaurus.etymology: From Ancient Greek styrax, "spike at the butt-end of a spear-shaft", combined with Greek sauros, "lizard" - means "spiked lizard"
Styracosaurus.description: Styracosaurus is an extinct genus of herbivorous dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous (Campanian stage) of North America. It had four to six long parietal spikes extending from its neck frill, a smaller jugal horn on each of its cheeks, and a single horn protruding from its nose, which may have been up to 60 centimeters (2 feet) long and 15 centimeters (6 inches) wide. The function or functions of the horns and frills have been debated for many years.
diagnostic_features: Nasal horn-core large, upright, straight, rising from back of nasals and positioned remotely from acute rostral apex
Spike-shaped projections on posterior margin of frill (three pairs on each side, tapering, projecting obliquely backward and outward)
Postfrontal fontanelle large and long
Squamosals quadrangular, entering largely into front part of frill
Supratemporal fossae opening widely behind
Supraorbital horn-core incipient (small smooth depression indicating minute horn-core)

Suchomimus.etymology: From Greek souchos ('crocodile') and Latin mimus ('mimic'), meaning 'crocodile mimic', alluding to its elongated skull and piscivorous adaptations
Suchomimus.description: Suchomimus is a genus of large theropod dinosaur that lived in what is now Niger during the Aptian to Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous period, 112 million years ago. The only known species is S. tenerensis, originally described in 1998 by paleontologist Paul Sereno and colleagues from several fossils discovered one year earlier in the Elrhaz Formation. Although these fossils come from multiple specimens, they represent one of the most anatomically well-documented spinosaurids. The animal's generic name, which means "crocodile mimic", alludes to its elongated skull and piscivorous adaptations, while the specific name refers to the Ténéré Desert, where the fossils were discovered.
diagnostic_features: Elongate posterolateral premaxillary process that nearly excludes maxilla from external naris
Broadened and heightened posterior dorsal, sacral, and anterior caudal neural spines
Robust humeral tuberosities
Hypertrophied ulnar olecranon process offset from humeral articulation
Hook-shaped radial ectepicondyle

species.name: Suchomimus tenerensis
species.etymology: Named for the Ténéré Desert of Niger, where the fossils were discovered in 1997.

holotype.material: Partial skeleton lacking the skull

Suchosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'souchos' (crocodile, after the Egyptian crocodile-god Sobek) and 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'crocodile lizard'.
Suchosaurus.description: Suchosaurus is a dubious genus of large theropod dinosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous in what is now Europe. The type species, S. cultridens, was first mentioned by Richard Owen at the British Association meeting in 1841 and formally described in his 1842 Report on British Fossil Reptiles, based on a chimeric assemblage of fossil teeth and vertebrae discovered in the Tilgate Forest of Sussex, England, in sediments of the Wealden Supergroup.
diagnostic_features: Crown laterally compressed and subincurved, with two opposite trenchant edges on concave and convex outlines (unlike gavials where compression is antero-posterior)
Crown sides traversed by a few longitudinal parallel ridges with regular intervals of ~1 line breadth, subsiding before reaching apex and sooner on convex side
Edges of crown not serrated (distinguishing it from Megalosaurus and Argenton Crocodile)
Referred vertebrae have biconcave articular ends, compressed wedge-shaped body with sides gently convex, and finely striated silky external surface at mid-body

species.name: Suchosaurus cultridens
species.etymology: From Latin 'culter' (knife) and 'dens' (tooth); meaning 'knife-toothed'.

holotype.material: A single tooth; laterally compressed crown with two trenchant edges and longitudinal parallel ridges.

Supersaurus.etymology: From Latin super, "above" or "super", combined with Greek sauros, "lizard" - means "super lizard", reflecting its enormous size
Supersaurus.description: Supersaurus is a genus of diplodocid sauropod dinosaur that lived in North America during the Late Jurassic period. The type species, S. vivianae, was first discovered by Vivian Jones of Delta, Colorado, in the middle Morrison Formation of Colorado in 1972. The fossil remains came from the Brushy Basin Member of the formation, dating between 153 and 145 million years ago. It is among the longest dinosaurs ever discovered, with the three known specimens reaching 33-40 meters (108-131 ft) in length, with the largest individual possibly exceeding 40 meters (130 ft) in size. Mass estimates for the WDC and BYU specimens tend to be around 35-44 metric tons (39-49 short tons) in body mass. A potential second species, S. lourinhanensis (Dinheirosaurus), is known from Portugal and has been dated to a similar time.
diagnostic_features: Shallow outward curve in inferior border of scapula at top of transverse ridge indicating ligament origin
Inferior border forming gentle curve from glenoid process to distal end, resembling Apatosaurus and Diplodocus more than Brachiosaurus or Camarasaurus
Inferior fossa longer than wide, contrasting with Apatosaurus and Camarasaurus design

Suskityrannus.etymology: From Zuni suski, "coyote", combined with Greek tyrannos, "tyrant" - means "coyote tyrant"
Suskityrannus.description: Suskityrannus is a genus of small tyrannosauroid theropod from the Late Cretaceous of southern Laramidia. It contains a single species, Suskityrannus hazelae, and the type specimen was found in the Turonian-aged Moreno Hill Formation of the Zuni Basin in western New Mexico.

Medial condyle of proximal tibia hooked posteromedially
D-shaped, incisiform and carinate premaxillary teeth
Anteroposteriorly shortened premaxilla (less than 10% of maxilla length)
Cervical vertebrae neural arches X-shaped in dorsal view with anteroposteriorly short neural spine
Arctometatarsalian pes with metatarsal III pinched between II and IV (earliest record in tyrannosauroids)

Suuwassea.etymology: From the Crow language, derived from 'suuwassa' meaning 'the first thunder heard in spring'; the root 'suu' means 'thunder' and 'wassa' means 'ancient', evoking the 'thunder lizard' epithet often applied to sauropods.
Suuwassea.description: Suuwassea is a genus of dicraeosaurid sauropod dinosaur found in Upper Jurassic strata of the Morrison Formation, located in southern Carbon County, Montana, United States. The fossil remains were recovered in a series of expeditions during a period spanning the years 1999 and 2000 and were described by J.D. Harris and Peter Dodson in 2004. They consist of a disarticulated but associated partial skeleton, including partial vertebral series and limb bones.
diagnostic_features: supraoccipital with ventral end drawn out into narrow, elongate process contributing minimally to foramen magnum margin
basioccipital not contributing to dorsal side of occipital condylar neck
antotic processes of laterosphenoid separated from frontals by deep notches
cranial cervical neural spines restricted to caudal halves of centra, craniocaudally compressed, expanded distally, and not bifurcate
distal caudal centra ("whiplash" form) amphiplatyan
dorsal tuberculum of humerus well developed
proximal articular surface of tibia wider mediolaterally than long craniocaudally
calcaneus spheroidal
pedal phalanges longer proximodistally than wide mediolaterally

Suzhousaurus.etymology: Named after Suzhou (a region in Gansu Province, China) where the fossils were found, combined with Greek sauros, "lizard" - means "Suzhou lizard"
Suzhousaurus.description: Suzhousaurus is an extinct genus of large therizinosaurid dinosaurs from the Early Cretaceous of China. The genus is known from two specimens discovered in the Xiagou and Zhonggou Formations, both part of the Xinminbao Group. These findings were made during fieldwork in 1999 and 2004.

Pubis with strongly concave cranial margin
Large therizinosauroid (humeral proximodistal length 550 mm)

Syngonosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'syngonos' meaning 'congenital' or 'related by birth', combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', likely referring to the fused or closely associated bones in the specimen.
Syngonosaurus.description: Syngonosaurus is an extinct genus of ornithopod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous. It was an iguanodontian discovered in the Cambridge Greensand of England and was first described in 1879. The type species, S. macrocercus, was described by British paleontologist Harry Seeley in 1879 and it was later synonymised with Acanthopholis, but the genus was reinstated in a 2020 study, when Syngonosaurus and Eucercosaurus were reinterpreted as basal iguanodontians.

Sharp keel developed on sacral vertebral centra
Caudal vertebrae with oblique, slightly procoelous articular faces indicating stiff tail
Large facets on caudal vertebrae for chevron bones arranged as sutural surfaces
Tail vertebrae compressed below transverse processes with well-rounded visceral surface

Szechuanosaurus.description: Szechuanosaurus is an extinct genus of carnivorous theropod dinosaur from China. Its type species is based on several undiagnostic teeth from the Kuangyuan Series. Potential specimens referred to the genus span from the Early Triassic through the Late Triassic. Additional possible specimens were also reported from the Kalaza Formation.

Tachiraptor.description: Tachiraptor is a genus of carnivorous theropod dinosaurs found in the early Jurassic period La Quinta Formation of Venezuela. It includes one species, Tachiraptor admirabilis, described from a fossilized tibia and ischium. They were small bipedal dinosaurs, with a deduced total body length of just over 1.5 m (4.9 ft).

Talarurus.etymology: From Greek talaros, "wicker basket", combined with Greek oura, "tail" - means "basket tail" or "wicker tail", referring to the club-like tail
Talarurus.description: Talarurus is a genus of ankylosaurid dinosaur that lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous period, about 96 million to 89 million years ago. The first remains of Talarurus were discovered in 1948 and later described by the Russian paleontologist Evgeny Maleev with the type species T. plicatospineus. It is known from multiple yet sparse specimens, making it one of the most well known ankylosaurines, along with Pinacosaurus. Elements from the specimens consists of various bones from the body; five skulls have been discovered and assigned to the genus, although the first two were very fragmented.

Talenkauen.description: Talenkauen is a genus of basal iguanodont dinosaur from the Campanian or Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous Cerro Fortaleza Formation, formerly known as the Pari Aike Formation of Patagonian Lake Viedma, in the Austral Basin of Santa Cruz, Argentina. It is based on MPM-10001A, a partial articulated skeleton missing the rear part of the skull, the tail, and the hands. The type and only species is Talenkauen santacrucensis.

Taleta.etymology: From Arabic 'taleta' (three), in reference to this being the third duck-billed dinosaur recovered from Couche III of the Moroccan phosphates, after Ajnabia odysseus and Minqaria bata.
Taleta.description: Taleta is an extinct genus of arenysaurin lambeosaurine hadrosaurid dinosaur from the late Maastrichtian Couche III of the Oulad Abdoun Basin (Sidi Chennane mines, Central Morocco), a shallow-marine phosphorite depositional setting. The single species, Taleta taleta, is known from associated left and right maxillae of a single individual (MHNM.KH.1557) preserving in-situ dentition; phylogenetic analysis recovers it within Arenysaurini, forming an African clade with Ajnabia odysseus and Minqaria bata. Longrich et al. (2025) interpret the three Moroccan arenysaurins as a dispersal-driven adaptive radiation seeded from southern Europe.

Alveolar margin higher laterally than medially, such that alveoli open ventrolaterally.
Single functional tooth per maxillary tooth family.
Maxillary teeth greatly enlarged, with crowns obliquely oriented and raked backwards relative to the alveolar margin.
Primary ridge of maxillary teeth extremely tall and prominent, roughly doubling the mediolateral width of the crown, and interlocking with the alveolar margin.
Toothrow very straight in both lateral and ventral views.

Talos.description: Talos is a genus of troodontid theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Kaiparowits Formation of Utah, United States. It contains a single species, Talos sampsoni, described from a partial skeleton in 2011. Talos was a small bipedal carnivore approximately 2 m long.

Tameryraptor.etymology: From Egyptian Tamery, meaning "the beloved land" (an ancient Egyptian name for Egypt), combined with Latin raptor, "thief" - means "thief from the beloved land"
Tameryraptor.description: Tameryraptor is an extinct genus of large carcharodontosaurid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous (Cenomanian age) in what is now Egypt. It is known from a partial skeleton collected in rock layers from the Bahariya Formation by crews of German paleontologist Ernst Stromer in 1914, comprising an incomplete skull, vertebrae, and several other postcranial elements. Stromer described the specimen in 1931, referring it to the previously named Megalosaurus saharicus on the basis of its tooth anatomy, and placing it in a new genus, Carcharodontosaurus. In 1944, it was destroyed in the Bombing of Munich during the Second World War. The specimen remained assigned to Carcharodontosaurus saharicus until a review of photographs of the fossil material in 2025 allowed researchers around German paleontologist Maximilian Kellermann to recognize the material as belonging to a distinct taxon known from a single species, Tameryraptor markgrafi.

Taohelong.etymology: From Chinese Tao (the Tao River), he ("river"), and long ("dragon") - means "dragon of the Tao River"
Taohelong.description: Taohelong is a genus of nodosaurid dinosaur known from Early Cretaceous rocks in north-central China. It is based on Gansu Dinosaur Museum (GSDM) 00021, fossils including a tail vertebra, ribs, a left ilium (the main bone of the hip), and bony armor recovered from the Hekou Group in the Lanzhou-Minhe Basin. The animal's armor includes part of a "sacral shield", a carpet of osteoderms over the hips found in some other ankylosaurians. Taohelong was named and described in 2013 by Yang Jing-Tao, You Hai-Lu, Li Da-Qing, and Kong De-Lai. The type species is Taohelong jinchengensis. The generic name means "dragon (long) of the river (he) Tao". The specific name refers to the provenance at Jincheng.

Tarbosaurus.etymology: From Ancient Greek 'tarbos' meaning 'terror' or 'alarm' and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Tarbosaurus.description: Tarbosaurus is a genus of large tyrannosaurid dinosaur that lived in Asia during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous epoch. It contains the type and single species Tarbosaurus bataar, which is known from the Nemegt Formation of Mongolia, with more fragmentary remains found further afield in the Subashi Formation of China. Tarbosaurus is represented by dozens of fossil specimens, including several complete skulls and skeletons. These remains have allowed studies focusing on its phylogeny, skull mechanics, and brain structure. Further fossil remains have been reported from other geologic formations of Asia, however, these remains are fragmentary and cannot be confidently assigned to Tarbosaurus or the type species.

Tastavinsaurus.etymology: Named in honor of the Rio Tastavins in Spain, where the fossils were found.
Tastavinsaurus.description: Tastavinsaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur belonging to the Titanosauriformes. It is based on a partial skeleton from the Early Cretaceous Xert Formation of Spain. The type species is Tastavinsaurus sanzi, named in honor of the Rio Tastavins in Spain and Spanish paleontologist José Luis Sanz. The genus is known from two specimens, one from the Xert Formation and one from the Forcall Formation. Tastavinsaurus was originally described as a somphospondylan, but it may be a brachiosaurid. The clade Laurasiformes was coined for Tastavinsaurus and its close relatives, which may include Cedarosaurus, Soriatitan, and Venenosaurus.

Taurovenator.etymology: From Latin 'taurus' meaning 'bull' and 'venator' meaning 'hunter', hence 'bull hunter'.
Taurovenator.description: Taurovenator, from Latin taurus, meaning "bull", and venator, meaning "hunter", is an extinct genus of large, probable carcharodontosaurid theropod dinosaurs that lived in what is now Argentina during the Cenomanian age of the Late Cretaceous, around 95 to 93.9 million years ago. Initially only known from a single postorbital skull bone described from the Huincul Formation, Taurovenator violantei was named in 2016 by Argentine paleontologist Matias Motta and colleagues. Debate came about over the validity of the species, with some paleontologists arguing that Taurovenator was synonymous with the earlier-named carcharodontosaurid Mapusaurus. However, the 2024 description of a well-preserved partial skull and skeleton referrable to Taurovenator aided in distinguishing the two taxa.

Tawa.etymology: Named after Tawa, the Hopi sun god, reflecting the Hopi people's connection to the American Southwest where the fossil was discovered in New Mexico.
Tawa.description: Tawa is a genus of possible basal theropod dinosaurs from the Late Triassic period. The fossil remains of Tawa hallae, the type and only species were found in the Hayden Quarry of Ghost Ranch, New Mexico, US. Its discovery alongside the relatives of Coelophysis and Herrerasaurus supports the hypothesis that the earliest dinosaurs arose in Gondwana during the early Late Triassic period in what is now South America, and radiated from there around the globe. The specific name honors Ruth Hall, founder of the Ghost Ranch Museum of Paleontology.

Tazoudasaurus.etymology: Named after Tazouda, one of the fossil localities near Toundoute in the High Atlas Mountains of Morocco, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'
Tazoudasaurus.description: Tazoudasaurus is a genus of gravisaurian (probably vulcanodontid) sauropod dinosaurs from the late Early Jurassic (Toarcian). It was recovered in the "Toundoute Continental Series" (Azilal Formation), located in the High Atlas Mountains of Morocco in North Africa. Along with Patagosaurus, Volkheimeria, Bagualia, and Perijasaurus (perhaps Barapasaurus and Kotasaurus as well), it represents one of the few sauropods named from this stage on Gondwana, as well as the only one from Africa.

Tenontosaurus.etymology: From Greek tenon ('sinew') and sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'sinew lizard', referring to the bony tendons stiffening its back and tail
Tenontosaurus.description: Tenontosaurus is a genus of iguanodontian ornithopod dinosaur. It had an unusually long, broad tail, which like its back was stiffened with a network of bony tendons. The genus is known from the late Aptian to Albian ages of the Early Cretaceous period sediments of western North America, dating between 115 and 108 million years ago. It contains two species, Tenontosaurus tilletti (described by John Ostrom in 1970) and Tenontosaurus dossi (described by Winkler, Murry, and Jacobs in 1997). Many specimens of T. tilletti have been collected from several geological formations throughout western North America. T. dossi is known from only a handful of specimens collected from the Twin Mountains Formation of Parker County, Texas.

Terminocavus.etymology: From Latin 'terminus' meaning 'end' and 'cavus' meaning 'cavity', meaning 'coming to the end of the cavity', referring to the nearly closed parietal embayment before its complete loss in more derived taxa
Terminocavus.description: Terminocavus is a genus of ceratopsid dinosaur from the late Cretaceous Period of what is now North America. The genus contains a single species, the type species Terminocavus sealeyi, known from a parietal and some other associated fragments. The holotype specimen was discovered in the Kirtland Formation of New Mexico in 1997, and was later described and named in a 2020 study. It was similar in anatomy to Pentaceratops and Anchiceratops, which it was closely related to, but had a distinctive heart-shaped upper frill with very narrow notch. It has been hypothesized to form an anagenetic series with several other chasmosaur species.

Tharosaurus.etymology: Named for the Thar Desert of Rajasthan, India, where the holotype was found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Tharosaurus.description: Tharosaurus is an extinct genus of potentially dubious eusauropod sauropod dinosaurs from the Middle Jurassic Jaisalmer Formation of India. The genus contains a single species, Tharosaurus indicus, known from a fragmentary skeleton including several vertebrae and a rib. When it was named in 2023, Tharosaurus was interpreted as the earliest known diplodocoid and the first member of this clade described from India. However, a later revision of the fossil material argued for a position outside of this clade, as an indeterminate eusauropod. This revision could not find unique features in the Tharosaurus specimen, so it was classified as a nomen dubium.

Thecocoelurus.etymology: A contraction of the genus names Thecospondylus and Coelurus, translating to 'sheathed hollow form', reflecting the specimen's dual taxonomic history under those two genera
Thecocoelurus.description: Thecocoelurus is a genus of theropod dinosaur from the early Cretaceous period of England. Its type specimen was discovered in strata from the Wessex Formation on the Isle of Wight by the Reverend William Fox, and after his death, it, alongside the rest of his collection, became the property of the British Museum of Natural History. The specimen was named in 1888 by Harry Govier Seeley, who assigned it to the genus Thecospondylus . In 1901, it was reassigned by Baron Franz Nopcsa to Coelurus. In 1923, the specimen was removed from either genus by Friedrich von Huene, who assigned it to a genus of its own. Thecocoelurus currently consists of one species, T. daviesi. The validity of the genus has been questioned, with a 2001 publication finding it to be a nomen dubium, although this treatment has not been maintained.

Thecodontosaurus.etymology: From Greek theke (case, socket), odous (tooth) and sauros (lizard); meaning "socket-tooth lizard", reflecting Riley and Stutchbury's observation that the teeth are set in distinct deep alveoli — a configuration unusual among the reptiles known to them at the time.
Thecodontosaurus.description: Thecodontosaurus is a genus of herbivorous basal sauropodomorph dinosaur that lived during the late Triassic period (Carnian age). Its remains are known mostly from Triassic "fissure fillings" in southern England. Thecodontosaurus was a small bipedal animal, about 2 m (6.6 ft) long. It is one of the first dinosaurs to be discovered and is one of the oldest that ever existed. Many species have been named within the genus, but only the type species Thecodontosaurus antiquus is seen as valid today.
diagnostic_features: Teeth set in deep, distinct alveoli to nearly half their length — the feature for which Riley and Stutchbury named the genus.
Hollow-rooted teeth in which a replacement crown forms within the same alveolar cavity as the functional tooth.
Tooth crowns lancet-shaped, with serrated anterior and posterior edges and serrations directed toward the apex.
Dentary short and deep, with maximum dorsoventral depth greater than 20% of dentary length.
All teeth retain a recurved lateral profile; the middle and posterior teeth do not become lanceolate as in other basal sauropodomorphs.
Posterior dorsal and anterior sacral centra with a keyhole-shaped neural canal in transverse section and an extensively ventrally excavated centrum.
Mid-caudal vertebrae with the anterior edge of the transverse process continuing as a sharp ridge across the neural arch.
Proximal caudal centra with the ventral furrowing reduced or lost; ventral surface transversely convex with a median ridge in at least one specimen.

Therizinosaurus.etymology: From Greek therizein ('to reap' or 'to cut') and sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'scythe lizard', named for its enormous scythe-like claws
Therizinosaurus.description: Therizinosaurus is a genus of very large therizinosaurid dinosaurs that lived during the Late Cretaceous period in what is now Asia. It contains a single species, Therizinosaurus cheloniformis, known from the fossiliferous Nemegt Formation. The first remains of Therizinosaurus were found in 1948 by a Mongolian field expedition in the Gobi Desert and later described by Evgeny Maleev in 1954. The genus is only known from a few bones, including gigantic manual unguals (claw bones), from which it gets its name, and additional findings comprising fore and hindlimb elements that were discovered from the 1960s through the 1980s.

Thescelosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'theskelos' meaning 'marvelous' or 'wondrous' and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', hence 'marvelous lizard'.
Thescelosaurus.description: Thescelosaurus is a genus of ornithischian dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period in western North America. It was named and described in 1913 by the paleontologist Charles W. Gilmore; the type species is T. neglectus. Two other species, T. garbanii and T. assiniboiensis, were named in 1976 and 2011, respectively. Additional species have been suggested but are currently not accepted. Thescelosaurus is the eponymous member of its family, the Thescelosauridae. Thescelosaurids are either considered to be basal ("primitive") ornithopods, or are placed outside of this group within the broader group Neornithischia.

Thyreosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'thyreos' meaning 'shield' (a large oblong shield) and 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', referring to the distinctive shield-like dermal armor of the animal.
Thyreosaurus.description: Thyreosaurus is an extinct genus of stegosaurian dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic El Mers III Formation of Morocco. The genus contains a single species, Thyreosaurus atlasicus, known from a partial disarticulated skeleton consisting of several dorsal vertebrae, ribs, a limb bone, and dermal bones. Thyreosaurus is characterized by a unique dermal armor with an asymmetrical texture, indicating that it may have been recumbent. Alongside Adratiklit, Thyreosaurus increases the diversity of unique stegosaurs occurring in the Middle Jurassic of Africa.

Tianyulong.etymology: From 'Tianyu' (the Shandong Tianyu Museum of Nature in Pingyi, where the holotype is housed) and Mandarin Chinese 'long' (dragon).
Tianyulong.description: Tianyulong is an extinct genus of heterodontosaurid ornithischian dinosaur from Jianchang County, western Liaoning Province, China. The single species, Tianyulong confuciusi, is known from a small (~70 cm) subadult skeleton (STMN 26-3) preserving partial cranium, postcranial skeleton, and three patches of filamentous integumentary structures along the neck, back, and tail. Zheng, You, Xu and Dong (2009) originally assigned the holotype to the Early Cretaceous Yixian Formation of the Jehol Group, but subsequent reassignment of the source horizon places it in the Middle-Late Jurassic Tiaojishan Formation. The filaments are unbranched, hollow, apparently rigid singular structures up to ~60 mm long; the authors did not claim homology with theropod protofeathers, noting closer morphological similarity to Psittacosaurus bristles and treating convergent acquisition as the default interpretation. Tianyulong is recovered as the basalmost well-known heterodontosaurid in the original phylogenetic analysis.

Tianyuraptor.etymology: Named after the Shandong Tianyu Museum of Nature where the holotype specimen is housed, combined with Latin 'raptor' meaning 'robber', referring to the action of grabbing prey
Tianyuraptor.description: Tianyuraptor is a genus of short-armed dromaeosaurid dinosaur ('running lizard'; a type of small dinosaur considered to be closely related to birds) that lived during the Early Cretaceous, about 122 million years ago. Its remains have been found in western Liaoning, China. It was similar to other dromaeosaurids found in Liaoning, with the exception of being somewhat more primitive. The type specimen, formally named in 2009, shows features not seen in previously known Northern Hemisphere (Laurasian) dromaeosaurids, but present in Southern Hemisphere (Gondwanan) species and early birds. Because of this, the scientists who first studied Tianyuraptor described it as a "transitional species", bridging the gap between northern and southern types of dromaeosaurid. Tianyuraptor also differs from previously known dromaeosaurids in that it possesses a relatively small furcula ("wishbone"), and unusually short forelimbs.

Tianzhenosaurus.etymology: From Tianzhen County (Shanxi Province, China, where the holotype was found) and Greek 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'Tianzhen lizard'.
Tianzhenosaurus.description: Tianzhenosaurus is a genus of ankylosaurid dinosaurs known from the Late Cretaceous Huiquanpu Formation of Shanxi Province, China. The genus contains two species, T. youngi (the type species) and T. chengi.
Tianzhenosaurus.dispute: The validity of Tianzhenosaurus is contested. Sullivan (1999) and Arbour and Currie (2015) treated T. youngi as a junior subjective synonym of the Mongolian ankylosaurid Saichania chulsanensis, finding no taxonomically significant differences between the holotype skulls. In 2024, Pang, Li and Guo described a second species, T. chengi, treating Tianzhenosaurus as a valid genus. No broad consensus has been reached.
diagnostic_features: Skull low, flat, medium-sized, isosceles triangle shape; skull roof covered with irregular bony tubercles.

Titanoceratops.etymology: From Greek 'titanos' meaning 'titan' (giant) and 'ceratops' meaning 'horned face', in reference to its exceptionally large size among horned dinosaurs.
Titanoceratops.description: Titanoceratops is a controversial genus of chasmosaurine ceratopsian dinosaur that lived in the Late Cretaceous period (Campanian stage, about 75 million years ago) in what is now New Mexico. Titanoceratops was named for its large size, being one of the largest known horned dinosaurs and the type species was named T. ouranos, after Uranus (Ouranos), the father of the Greek titans. It was named in 2011 by Nicholas R. Longrich for a specimen previously referred to Pentaceratops. Longrich believed that unique features found in the skull reveal it to have been a close relative of Triceratops, classified within the subgroup Triceratopsini. However, other researchers have expressed skepticism, and believe Titanoceratops to simply be an unusually large, old specimen of Pentaceratops.

Tonganosaurus.etymology: Named for the town of Tong'an in Sichuan Province, China, near where it was found, plus Greek sauros ('lizard')
Tonganosaurus.description: Tonganosaurus is a genus of mamenchisaurid sauropod dinosaur, similar to Omeisaurus. It is known from one specimen consisting of twenty vertebrae, a front limb and pectoral girdle, and a complete hind limb with partial hip. It was discovered in the Yimen Formation, China. The horizon of the specimen and the age of the Yimen Formation is controversial. The formation has been divided into three levels, and Tonganosaurus appears to be of late Early Jurassic (Pliensbachian) in age. Tonganosaurus is the oldest known member of the mamenchisaurids, being almost 15 million years older than the next-oldest members of the group. It was first named by Li Kui, Yang Chun-Yan, Liu Jian, and Wang Zheng-Xin in 2010, and the type species is Tonganosaurus hei.

Fossils have been discovered across the Western Interior of North America, from as far north as Saskatchewan to as far south as Texas.

Trachodon.etymology: From Greek trachys (rough) and odon (tooth); meaning "rough tooth", referring to the granulated inner surface of the hadrosaurid tooth Leidy described.
Trachodon.description: Trachodon is a dubious genus of hadrosaurid dinosaur from the Upper Cretaceous of what is now Montana in the western United States. The only species is T. mirabilis, though many others have been assigned to the genus. T. mirabilis was described by Joseph Leidy in 1856 based on a set of teeth; however, this was later shown to be a mixture of hadrosaurid and ceratopsian teeth. These fossils were unearthed in 1856 by Ferdinand Vandeveer Hayden during an expedition to the Missouri River in Montana, USA, in rock from the Judith River Formation. This formation dates to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, which lasted from 79 to 75.3 million years ago. One of the teeth, an incomplete hadrosaurid tooth, was later chosen as the holotype.

The type and only species is Tralkasaurus cuyi, named in 2020 by Mauricio Cerroni and colleagues based on an incomplete skeleton. A medium-sized abelisaurid, Tralkasaurus exhibits a conflicting blend of characteristics found among the early-diverging abelisauroids with others that characterize the highly specialized clade Brachyrostra, and thus its position within the clade is poorly-resolved.

Triceratops.etymology: From Greek tri (three), keras (horn) and ops (face); meaning "three-horned face", referring to the paired supraorbital horn-cores and the median nasal horn-core that ornament the skull.
Triceratops.description: Triceratops is the best-known ceratopsid dinosaur and among the most recognizable of all non-avian dinosaurs, defined by its three large facial horns, prominent toothless beak and solid, unfenestrated parietal-squamosal frill. Marsh erected the genus in 1889 by transferring his earlier Ceratops horridus (Marsh, 1888) to the new combination Triceratops horridus, on a partial skull (later cataloged YPM 1820) recovered from the "Laramie" — now Lance — Formation of Wyoming. Through the 1890s and early 1900s Marsh and others named more than a dozen further species, of which only two are currently accepted today (T. horridus, the type, and T. prorsus), both restricted to the latest Maastrichtian of the Western Interior of North America. Forster (1996) sank most nominal species into one of these two through a cladistic and morphometric revision; Scannella et al. (2014) subsequently documented a stratigraphic pattern in the Hell Creek Formation suggesting a primarily anagenetic transition from T. horridus low in the section to T. prorsus near the K-Pg boundary. Several other names (T. galeus, T. sulcatus, T. maximus, T. eurycephalus, T. albertensis) rest on inadequate material and are now treated as nomina dubia. The proposed synonymy of Torosaurus with mature Triceratops (Scannella and Horner, 2010) has not been broadly accepted in subsequent literature (Longrich and Field 2012; Maiorino et al. 2013) and is not adopted here.
diagnostic_features: Three large facial horns: paired supraorbital horn-cores plus a median nasal horn formed by the epinasal, seated on coossified nasals.
Edentulous premaxillae fronting an unpaired rostral bone (os rostrale) anterior to the premaxillae, forming a projecting toothless beak.
Parietal-squamosal frill solid and unfenestrated, extremely thick and heavily vascularised on its dorsal surface.
Squamosal short and broad with convex, rounded lateral margins; never thinned or fenestrated.
Frill saddle-shaped in dorsal aspect, with an upturned caudal margin and a strong parietal midline ridge.
Epoccipital ossifications fused along the parietal-squamosal margin, with one epoccipital spanning the midline of the parietal.
Frontal fontanelle small and circular, or absent in mature individuals, due to closure of the frontoparietal sutures.
Huge occipital portion of the frill extending posteriorly and laterally, bent ventrally at the sides to overhang the neck.

Trigonosaurus.etymology: From Greek 'trigōnon' (triangle), in reference to the Triângulo Mineiro region of Minas Gerais, Brazil where the holotype was found, and 'sauros' (lizard); meaning 'triangle lizard'.
Trigonosaurus.description: Trigonosaurus is a genus of saltasaurid dinosaurs from the Maastrichtian Serra da Galga Formation of Brazil. The type species, Trigonosaurus pricei, was first described by Campos, Kellner, Bertini, and Santucci in 2005. It was based on two specimens, both consisting mainly of vertebrae. The two specimens were originally believed to have come from the same individual. However, one specimen was described as the holotype of Caieiria in 2022, while the holotype may have instead come from Baurutitan. Before its description, it was known as the "Peirópolis titanosaur", after the place it was found.
Trigonosaurus.dispute: The validity of Trigonosaurus is contested. Silva Junior et al. (2022) proposed that T. pricei is a junior subjective synonym of Baurutitan britoi (which has page priority within the same 2005 journal volume) and erected the postcranial paratype (MCT 1719-R) as a separate new genus, Caieiria allocaudata. Fronimos (2023) explicitly rejected the synonymy, citing morphological differences in the first caudal vertebra of the two taxa.

Anterior caudal vertebrae (2-5) with two pronounced dorsal depressions on the transverse process; middle caudals with one such depression.
Prezygapophyses on caudal vertebrae extended forward with wide articular faces.

Articular surfaces for haemal arches strongly developed from caudal 3 through the last preserved element (caudal 20); transverse processes well developed throughout the anterior and medial caudal sequence.

Trinisaura.description: Trinisaura is a genus of ornithopod dinosaur that lived during the late Campanian stage of the Upper Cretaceous, around 73 to 72 million years ago in what is now James Ross Island off the coast of northern Antarctica near Patagonia. It is known from a single, incomplete postcranial skeleton that includes several vertebrae, a partial pelvis, and nearly complete right hindlimb. The fossils were collected in 2008 by paleontologists Juan Moly and Rodolfo Coria from the sandstone of the Snow Hill Island Formation. It remained undescribed in the collections of the Museo de La Plata until its description by Coria and colleagues in 2013, being the basis of the novel genus and species Trinisaura santamartaensis. The genus name is to commemorate the efforts of Argentine geologist Trinidad "Trini" Diaz and the Latin root -sauros, meaning "lizard". The species name is after Santa Marta Cove, where the fossils were collected.

Triunfosaurus.etymology: Named for the Triunfo Basin in Paraíba, Brazil, where the fossils were found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.

It contains a single species, T. leonardii, described by Carvalho et al. in 2017. As a genus, Triunfosaurus can be distinguished from all other titanosaurs by the unique proportions of its ischium. It was initially described as a basal titanosaur, making it the earliest basal titanosaur known; however, subsequent research questioned the identification of the taxon as a titanosaur, instead reassigning it to the Somphospondyli.

Tsintaosaurus.etymology: Named for the city of Qingdao (formerly romanized as Tsintao), China, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Tsintaosaurus.description: Tsintaosaurus is a genus of hadrosaurid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of China. It was about 8.3 meters (27 ft) long and weighed 2.5 tonnes (2.8 short tons). The type species is Tsintaosaurus spinorhinus, first described by Chinese paleontologist C. C. Young in 1958. As a hadrosaur, Tsintaosaurus had the characteristic 'duck bill' snout and a battery of powerful teeth which it used to chew vegetation. It usually walked on all fours, but could rear up on its hind legs to scout for predators and flee when it spotted one. Like other hadrosaurs, Tsintaosaurus probably lived and traveled in herds.

Tyrannosaurus.etymology: From Greek tyrannos (tyrant) and sauros (lizard); meaning "tyrant lizard", a name Osborn coined to convey the genus's exceptional size relative to all then-known carnivorous land vertebrates.
Tyrannosaurus.description: Tyrannosaurus is the type genus of Tyrannosauridae and one of the most iconic non-avian dinosaurs, defined by a deep, massively built skull, a foreshortened presacral column of about 23 vertebrae, an extremely reduced two-fingered forelimb, and a heavy, columnar hindlimb terminating in a functionally tridactyl pes. Osborn erected the genus and its type species T. rex in 1905 on a partial skeleton (then cataloged AMNH 973, now CM 9380) collected by Barnum Brown in 1902 from the Hell Creek beds of Dawson County, Montana. In the same paper Osborn also named Dynamosaurus imperiosus on a Wyoming skeleton (AMNH 5866), then formally sank it into Tyrannosaurus rex the following year. The mounted AMNH 5027 specimen, monographed by Osborn in 1916, became the public face of the genus for most of the twentieth century. The original AMNH 973 holotype was sold to the Carnegie Museum during World War II and became CM 9380. Cope's earlier name Manospondylus gigas (1892), based on lost dorsal vertebrae from the Hell Creek of South Dakota, was eventually declared a nomen oblitum because Tyrannosaurus has been in continuous use as the senior available name for over fifty years (ICZN Article 23.9). Modern work compiled by Brusatte et al. (2010) established T. rex as the largest Maastrichtian theropod of Laramidia, with a maximum body length around 13 m, growth rates on the order of 0.7 t per year through a fast-growth phase, and bite forces in excess of 13 kN.
diagnostic_features: Megalocephalic skull with deep, massively built proportions, brought close to the sacrum by a shortened presacral column of approximately 23 vertebrae.
Fused nasals forming an arched midline ridge on the snout that reinforces the skull against bite-induced stress.
Teeth heterodont and broadly oval to D-shaped in cross-section, with transverse diameter exceeding anteroposterior; alveolar reinforcing plates on the inner surface of the maxilla and dentary.
Squamosal bearing a distinctive horizontal anterior bar projecting into the laterotemporal fenestra.
Forelimb extremely reduced; functionally didactyl manus with powerful recurved unguals; humerus little more than half the length of the femur.
Five sacral vertebrae coossified into a single neural plate with three small fenestrations between S2 and S5.
Pubis, ilium and ischium firmly coalesced; pubis terminating distally in a hugely expanded pedicle ("pubic boot").
Caudal series of approximately 53 vertebrae forming a long, flexible balancing tail without the rod-like rigidity of ornithomimids.

Tyrannotitan.etymology: From Greek tyrannos ('tyrant') and titan ('giant'), meaning 'tyrant titan'
Tyrannotitan.description: Tyrannotitan is a genus of large theropod dinosaur belonging to the carcharodontosaurid family. It is known from a single species, T. chubutensis, which lived during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous period in what is now Argentina. Tyrannotitan is considered to share a close relationship with other prominent South American carcharodontosaurids such as Giganotosaurus and Mapusaurus. Unlike its relatives, it was bulkier and more robust. This taxon is known from two specimens, both of which are highly incomplete.

Uberabatitan.etymology: Named after Uberaba, the city in Minas Gerais, Brazil where it was found, combined with Greek titan meaning 'giant'; translates as 'Uberaba titan'
Uberabatitan.description: Uberabatitan is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Brazil. It is known from bones including neck, back, and tail vertebrae, pelvic bones, and limb bones. These fossils were found in the uppermost portion of the Maastrichtian-age Serra da Galga Formation of the Bauru Group, in Uberaba, Minas Gerais. The type species, described by Salgado and Carvalho in 2008, is U. ribeiroi. To date, it is the most recent titanosaur from Bauru Group rocks; other titanosaurs from the Bauru Group, including Baurutitan and Trigonosaurus, come from lower (thus older) levels.

Mid-dorsals with robust composite lateral lamina formed mainly by diapophyseal lamina and relic spinodiapophyseal lamina
Mid and posterior dorsals with neural accessory laminae parallel to prespinal lamina (probable spinoprezygapophyseal laminae)
Mid-caudal centra with deeply excavated lateral faces
Pubis notably thick and robust with very stout longitudinal crest on external (ventral) face
Tibia with very robust lateral protuberance articulating with equally robust medial knob of fibula

Udanoceratops.etymology: Named for the Udan-Sayr locality in Mongolia where the holotype was found, combined with Greek 'keras' meaning 'horn' and 'ops' meaning 'face'.
Udanoceratops.description: Udanoceratops is a genus of large leptoceratopsid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous period of Mongolia. The holotype specimen, the partial skeleton of an adult with its bones encapsulated in calcium carbonate, was discovered in the 1980s as part of the Joint Soviet-Mongolian Paleontological Expedition, and was subsequently transported to the Paleontological Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences. In 1992, it was described by paleontologist Sergei Kurzanov. The sole species of Udanoceratops, also the type species, is Udanoceratops tschizhovi, named after a colleague of Kurzanov, D. O. Tschizhov. Additional remains have been assigned to Udanoceratops, though these may be misattributions.

Udelartitan.etymology: Combines 'UdelaR', an acronym for the Universidad de la República of Uruguay, with 'titan', a common suffix for large sauropod names referencing the pre-Olympian Titans of Greek mythology
Udelartitan.description: Udelartitan is an extinct genus of saltasauroid titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Guichón Formation of Uruguay. The genus contains a single species, U. celeste, known from fragmentary remains of at least two individuals.

Anterior caudal vertebrae with well-developed quadrangular neural spines and postspinal laminae

Middle caudal centra cotyles and condyles with hexagonal contour (autapomorphy)
Well developed fibular knob on posteromedial edge of fibula
Pyramidal astragalus
Marked oblique ridges on anterior face of metatarsals I and II (autapomorphy)

Ultrasaurus.etymology: From Latin ultra (beyond, exceeding) and Greek sauros (lizard); meaning "ultra lizard", reflecting Kim's inference that the animal exceeded Supersaurus in size.
Ultrasaurus.description: Ultrasaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur discovered by Haang Mook Kim in South Korea. However, the name was first used unofficially (as a nomen nudum) in 1979 by Jim Jensen to describe a set of giant dinosaur bones he discovered in the United States. Because Kim published the name for his specimen before Jensen could do so officially, George Olshevsky renamed the specimen as Ultrasauros. Jensen's giant sauropod was later found to be a chimera, and the type remains are now assigned to Supersaurus.
diagnostic_features: Ulna estimated total length ~118 cm, with proximal epiphysis long axis of 42 cm — larger than any known sauropod including Supersaurus
Distal long axis of ulna (~55 cm) equals the distal femur long axis of Supersaurus, implying a much larger overall body size
Neural spine of caudal vertebra (DGBU-1978A) 17.0 cm long, 11.5 cm wide, 4.5 cm wider than equivalent element in Mamenchisaurus hochuanensis

species.name: Ultrasaurus tabriensis
species.etymology: From Tabri (Tabri station, near the type locality at Bongam pass) and Latin -ensis ("from"); meaning "from Tabri".

holotype.institution: Department of Geology, Busan National University
holotype.material: Partial bone identified by Kim as a right ulna (preserved length 70 cm, estimated ~118 cm complete); later workers reinterpret the element as a humerus, yielding much smaller body-size estimates and rendering the genus a nomen dubium.

Ulughbegsaurus.etymology: Named after Ulugh Beg (the 15th-century Timurid sultan and astronomer), combined with Greek sauros meaning 'lizard'; translates as 'Ulugh Beg's lizard'
Ulughbegsaurus.description: Ulughbegsaurus is an extinct genus of carcharodontosaurid theropod dinosaurs from the Late Cretaceous Bissekty Formation (Turonian age) and Khodzhakul Formation (Cenomanian age) of Uzbekistan. The genus contains a single species, Ulughbegsaurus uzbekistanensis, known from multiple maxilla fragments.

Tubercles along with ridged rim of the antorbital fossa
Vertically oriented ridges on the lateral surface of maxilla

Rugose lateral surface texture characteristic of Carcharodontosauria

Unaysaurus.etymology: From 'unay', a word meaning 'black water' in the Tupi language indigenous to Brazil, referring to the black-water stream near the discovery site, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Unaysaurus.description: Unaysaurus is a genus of herbivorous unaysaurid sauropodomorph dinosaur. Discovered in southern Brazil, in the geopark of Paleorrota, in 1998, and announced in a press conference on Thursday, December 3, 2004, it is one of the oldest dinosaurs known. It is closely related to plateosaurid dinosaurs found in Germany, which indicates that it was relatively easy for species to spread across the giant landmass of the time, the supercontinent of Pangaea. The fossils of Unaysaurus are well-preserved. They consist of an almost complete skull, including a lower jaw, and partial skeleton with many of the bones still connected to each other in their natural positions. It is one of the most complete dinosaur skeletons (including complete skull) ever recovered in Brazil.
diagnostic_features: Well developed laterodorsally oriented process formed by frontal and parietal (more developed than in Plateosaurus)
Medial depression on mediodorsal surface of the parietals
Two fossae on the maxillary medial lamina
Deep ventral depression on the basisphenoid
Conspicuous blunt ridge running on lateral surface of deltopectoral crest

Unenlagia.etymology: From Mapuche 'unum' meaning 'bird' and 'llag' meaning 'half', meaning 'half-bird', reflecting its interpreted transitional position between birds and basal theropods.
Unenlagia.description: Unenlagia is a genus of unenlagiine theropod dinosaur that lived in South America during the Late Cretaceous period. The genus Unenlagia has been assigned two species: U. comahuensis, the type species described by Novas and Puerta in 1997, and U. paynemili, described by Calvo et al. in 2004.

Deep lateral pits in base of neural spines of posterior dorsals and anterior sacrals
Twisted scapular shaft with dorsal-facing external surface
Inflected dorsal margin of postacetabular iliac blade
Laterally oriented humeral articulation of scapula (previously unreported in non-avian dinosaurs)
Laterally oriented glenoid cavity enabling avian-style forelimb folding and elevation

Unescoceratops.description: Unescoceratops is a genus of leptoceratopsid ceratopsian dinosaurs known from the Late Cretaceous of Alberta, southern Canada. It contains a single species, Unescoceratops koppelhusae.

Unquillosaurus.etymology: Named for the Unquillo River of Salta Province, Argentina, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Unquillosaurus.description: Unquillosaurus is a genus of large theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Los Blanquitos Formation of Salta Province, Argentina. Its precise classification is uncertain, but most researchers consider it as a maniraptoran. The genus contains a single species, U. ceibalii, known only from a single fossilized pubis (a pelvic bone).
