Urbacodon.etymology: Named after URBAC (an acronym honoring Uzbek, Russian, British, American, and Canadian scientists who collaborated on Central Asian paleontological expeditions), combined with Greek odon meaning 'tooth'
Urbacodon.description: Urbacodon is a genus of troodontid theropod dinosaur. Two species have been described, both of which are known from a partial dentary: U. itemirensis from the Dzharakuduk Formation (Cenomanian) of Uzbekistan and U. norelli from the Iren Dabasu Formation of China. Possible remains are also known from the Bissekty Formation (Turonian) of Uzbekistan.

Dentary with 32 teeth arranged with diastema in posterior tooth row, more plesiomorphic than Troodon and Saurornithoides
Fewer neurovascular foramina in lateral groove and more bulbous anterior dentary crowns than Byronosaurus
Much larger size than Mei, distinguished by overall skeletal proportions
Distinct paradental groove structure unique among troodontids: deep cleft lingual to tooth row with narrow dorsal groove along dentary surface

Utahceratops.etymology: From 'Utah', the U.S. state where the fossil was found, and Greek 'keras' (stem 'cerat') meaning 'horn' and 'ops' meaning 'face', hence 'Utah horned face'.
Utahceratops.description: Utahceratops is an extinct genus of ceratopsian dinosaur that lived approximately 76.4~75.5 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous period in what is now Utah. Utahceratops was a large-sized, robustly-built, ground-dwelling, quadrupedal herbivore, that could grow up to an estimated 4.5-5 m (15-16 ft) long.

Utahraptor.etymology: Named for the state of Utah, USA, where the fossils were found, combined with Latin 'raptor' meaning 'robber' or 'plunderer'.
Utahraptor.description: Utahraptor is a genus of large dromaeosaurid (a group of feathered carnivorous theropods) dinosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous period from around 139 to 135 million years ago in what is now the United States. The genus was described in 1993 by American paleontologist James Kirkland and colleagues with the type species Utahraptor ostrommaysi, based on fossils that had been unearthed earlier from the Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah. Later, many additional specimens were described including those from the skull and postcranium in addition to those of younger individuals.

Utetitan.etymology: From 'Ute', honoring the original Ute peoples of central Utah on whose ancestral lands the holotype was recovered, and Greek 'titan' (giant).
Utetitan.description: Utetitan is an extinct genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the late Maastrichtian (Late Cretaceous) of southwestern North America. The single species, Utetitan zellaguymondeweyae, is based on USNM 15560 — a partial postcranial skeleton from the lower North Horn Formation at Joe's Valley on the Wasatch Plateau, Emery County, Utah — formerly the primary referred specimen of Alamosaurus sanjuanensis. Paul (2025) split this material away from Alamosaurus on the basis of scapular and ischial autapomorphies, restricted A. sanjuanensis to its New Mexican type horizon, and erected the new subfamily Utetitaninae for the new genus; that clade-name is single-paper-recent and not adopted as a parent here per the project's taxonomy policy.
diagnostic_features: Acromion process of the scapula strongly prominent.
Posterior profile of the scapula strongly sinuous, producing a prominent triangular glenoid process.
Paired tubercles dorsal to the scapular glenoid fairly prominent and widely separated.
Postero-dorsal edge of the scapular blade flares prominently posteriorly.
Lateral process of the ischium modest in size.
Postero-lateral profile of the ischium moderately concave-arced.

species.name: Utetitan zellaguymondeweyae
species.etymology: Honors Zella Guymon Dewey (1901-2002), the author's maternal grandmother, born in Huntington, Utah — approximately 30 km from the USNM 15560 quarry.

location.locality: Joe's Valley, Wasatch Plateau, Emery County

holotype.institution: National Museum of Natural History, Smithsonian Institution
holotype.material: Partial postcranial skeleton including dorsal ribs, caudals 1-30, 25 chevrons, both sternals, the right scapulocoracoid, humerus, radius, ulna, metacarpus, both ischia, and an associated osteoderm.

species.authors: Paul, Gregory S.

references.title: Stratigraphic and anatomical evidence for multiple titanosaurid dinosaur taxa in the Late Cretaceous (Campanian-Maastrichtian) of southwestern North America

Vagaceratops.etymology: From Latin vagus ('wandering') and Greek keratops ('horned face'), meaning 'wandering horned face', in reference to its close relationship with Kosmoceratops from Utah
Vagaceratops.description: Vagaceratops is a genus of chasmosaurine ceratopsid dinosaur which lived during the Late Cretaceous period (late Campanian) in what is now Alberta. Its fossils have been recovered from the Upper Dinosaur Park Formation. It is sometimes included in the genus Chasmosaurus as Chasmosaurus irvinensis instead of being recognized as its own genus.
diagnostic_features: Jugal notch on proximal squamosal broadly rounded and open (not parallel sided)
Transverse parietal bar straight
Epiparietals (ep1-ep3) and epiparietosquamosal (eps) short, forming recurved flat laminae
Predentary length one half that of dentary

Valdoraptor.etymology: From Latin 'Valdus' (Wealden, referring to the Wealden Group) and 'raptor' (plunderer); meaning 'Wealden plunderer'.
Valdoraptor.description: Valdoraptor is a genus of ornithomimosaurian theropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of England. It is known only from bones of the feet. The holotype, BMNH R2559 (incorrectly given by Owen as BMNH R2556), was found near Cuckfield in layers of the Tunbridge Wells Sand Formation dating from the late Valanginian. The specimen is damaged, lacking parts of the upper and lower ends. It has a conserved length of 21.5 centimeters (8.5 in) and an estimated total length of 24 centimeters (9.4 in). This genus is paleontologically significant for being the first ornithomimosaur specimen known from England and represents the earliest record of ornithomimosaurs.
diagnostic_features: Metatarsal II mediolaterally compressed.
Prominent dorsolateral ridge on metatarsal II.

Valdosaurus.etymology: From 'valdo', a modification of Old English 'weald' meaning 'a wood' (referring to the Weald region of England), combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Valdosaurus.description: Valdosaurus is a genus of bipedal herbivorous dryosaurid dinosaur known from the Early Cretaceous of the Isle of Wight and elsewhere in England. Originally its remains were believed to belong to Hypsilophodon. In 1889, Richard Lydekker assigned them to Camptosaurus, alongside a partial lower jaw, and applied the name Camptosaurus valdensis. In the 1970s, Peter Galton reassigned these remains to a new species of Dryosaurus, then to an entirely new genus and species, that being Valdosaurus proper. The type and only species of Valdosaurus, named by Galton, is V. canaliculatus.

Vectaerovenator.etymology: Named after Vectis (the Latin name for the Isle of Wight), combined with Latin aero meaning 'air' (referring to the pneumaticity of the vertebrae) and venator meaning 'hunter'; translates as 'Isle of Wight air-filled hunter'
Vectaerovenator.description: Vectaerovenator is a genus of tetanuran theropod from the Early Cretaceous period of what is now England (Lower Greensand Group; Ferruginous Sands). It contains one species, Vectaerovenator inopinatus; its holotype, consisting of the specimens IWCMS 2020.400, 2020.407, and 2019.84, comprises two anterior dorsal vertebrae, a cervical vertebra and a mid‐caudal vertebra from the late Aptian Ferruginous Sands of the Isle of Wight in southern England, discovered in 2019. Comparative anatomical analysis shows that this taxon shares homoplastic features with megalosauroids, carcharodontosaurs, and some coelurosaurs, and cannot be reliably placed beyond Tetanurae incertae sedis, but has enough autapomorphies that it can be considered a valid genus.

Velociraptor.etymology: From Latin velox (swift) and raptor (thief, plunderer); meaning "swift thief", chosen by Osborn to evoke the rapid, predatory habits inferred from the holotype's slender skull and recurved unguals.
Velociraptor.description: Velociraptor is a small dromaeosaurid theropod from the late Campanian of central Asia, defined by a long, low skull, recurved serrated teeth, and a hyperextensible sickle-clawed second pedal digit. Osborn erected the genus and the type species V. mongoliensis in 1924 on a partial skull and front-limb claw collected by Peter Kaisen in August 1923 at the Flaming Cliffs (Shabarakh Usu / Bayn Dzak) of the Djadokhta Formation in central Mongolia, during the Central Asiatic Expedition of the American Museum of Natural History. Soviet-Mongolian expeditions during the 1960s-70s recovered substantially more material, culminating in the famous "Fighting Dinosaurs" specimen (MPC-D 100/25), a near-complete skeleton of V. mongoliensis preserved in a death struggle with a Protoceratops andrewsi from Tugrugeen Shire. Barsbold (1983) reviewed the new material and erected Velociraptorinae for the genus. Turner et al. (2007) reported quill knobs on the ulna of a V. mongoliensis specimen, providing direct anatomical evidence for pennaceous wing feathering — making Velociraptor one of the better-attested feathered non-avian dinosaurs. Velociraptor's cultural prominence outside paleontology stems primarily from its oversized depiction in the Jurassic Park franchise, which conflates V. mongoliensis with the much larger Deinonychus antirrhopus.
diagnostic_features: Long, low skull with elongated face and greatly enlarged orbits; faciocranial index approximately 170%.
Postorbital region of the cranium extremely abbreviated; jaws excessively long and slender.
Teeth recurved and unilaterally or bilaterally serrate, set in relatively wide interdental spaces; about 11 maxillary and 14 dentary teeth.
Pronounced lacrimal boss at the dorsal margin of the preorbital bar; lacrimal broadly exposed on the skull roof.
Cervical centra with strongly developed epipophyses overhanging the postzygapophyseal facets; axis centrum pneumatic.
Anterior caudal vertebrae bearing elongate ossified tendons of the prezygapophyses and chevrons that form a stiffening sheath over 8-10 caudals.
Pelvis opisthopubic and dolichoiliac, with the pubis directed posteroventrally and a shortened ischium bearing a distally placed obturator process.
Pedal digit II hyperextensible and bearing an enlarged, sickle-shaped predatory ungual; metatarsal III mediolaterally pinched proximally and slightly shorter than II and IV.

Venenosaurus.etymology: From the Poison Strip Member of the Cedar Mountain Formation (Latin venenum, 'poison') where the fossils were found, plus Greek sauros ('lizard'), meaning 'poison lizard'
Venenosaurus.description: Venenosaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur that lived in what is now Utah during the Early Cretaceous. Its type and only species is Venenosaurus dicrocei. Fossils of Venenosaurus were first discovered in 1998, by Denver Museum of Natural History volunteer Anthony DiCroce, and described as a new genus and species in 2001 by Virginia Tidwell and colleagues, who named the species for DiCroce. Venenosaurus was a relatively small sauropod, and was similar to Cedarosaurus, another sauropod from the Early Cretaceous of Utah.

Vespersaurus.description: Vespersaurus is a genus of noasaurid theropod dinosaur from the Cretaceous Rio Paraná Formation in the Paraná Basin, Brazil. The type and only species is V. paranaensis, which would have lived in the giant prehistoric Botucatu Desert.

Vitosaura.etymology: Named in honor of Victoria 'Doña Vito' Romero, a 19th-century soldier born in the Los Llanos region near the type locality, combined with 'saura', feminine of Ancient Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Vitosaura.description: Vitosaura is an extinct genus of abelisaurid theropod dinosaurs known from the Late Cretaceous Los Llanos Formation of Argentina. The genus contains a single species, Vitosaura colozacani, known from a partial skeleton. Alongside Guemesia and the noasaurid Noasaurus, Vitosaura is one of the only Argentinian ceratosaurians found outside of Patagonia.

Volgatitan.etymology: Named for the Volga River region of Russia (Ulyanovsk Oblast) where the fossils were found, combined with 'titan' meaning 'giant'.
Volgatitan.description: Volgatitan is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of the Ulyanovsk Oblast, Russia. The type and only species is Volgatitan simbirskiensis, known from seven caudal vertebrae from a single individual. It is the oldest known titanosaur from the northern hemisphere, and is considered important for being related to the Lognkosauria, a group known only from South America later in the Late Cretaceous. It was first described in November 2018 by Russian paleontologists Alexander Averianov and Vladimir Efimov. It is estimated to have weighed about 17.3 metric tons (19.1 short tons).

Vouivria.etymology: Named after the vouivre, a mythological serpentine or dragon-like creature from the folklore of Franche-Comté, France, where the fossil was found
Vouivria.description: Vouivria is a genus of herbivorous sauropod dinosaur, belonging to the Brachiosauridae, that lived in the area of present France during the Late Jurassic. The type and only known species is Vouivria damparisensis. It is based on a specimen once commonly referred to as the "French Bothriospondylus" in the scientific literature, as the specimen was once identified as Bothriospondylus madagascariensis, a species known from the Middle Jurassic of Madagascar.

Wellnhoferia.description: Wellnhoferia is a genus of early prehistoric bird-like theropod dinosaur closely related to Archaeopteryx. It is known from a single species, W. grandis, that lived in what is now Germany, during the Late Jurassic. While Wellnhoferia was similar to Archaeopteryx, it had a shorter tail and its fourth toe was shorter than that of Archaeopteryx. Andrzej Elżanowski (2001) of the Institute of Zoology of the University of Wrocław, Poland, determined the differences resulted from a "phylogenetic reduction rather than individual variation."

Dorsal vertebrae with shallow fossa on lateral surface of neural arch at transverse process base

Femur with open cranial intercondylar groove

Wintonotitan.etymology: Named after Winton, Queensland, Australia (the area where it was found, associated with the Winton Formation), combined with Greek titan meaning 'giant'; translates as 'Winton titan'
Wintonotitan.description: Wintonotitan is a genus of titanosauriform dinosaur from the Cenomanian-aged (Late Cretaceous) Winton Formation of Australia. It is known from partial postcranial remains.

Scapula long with broad acromial blade and mid-scapular blade ridge
Humerus gracile with low narrow deltopectoral crest terminating proximal to mid-shaft

Wudingloong.etymology: From 'Wuding' (Wuding County, Yunnan Province, China, where the type locality lies) and Mandarin Chinese 'loong' (dragon).
Wudingloong.description: Wudingloong is an extinct genus of early-diverging massopodan sauropodomorph dinosaur from the Hettangian-early Sinemurian (Early Jurassic) Yubacun Formation at Wande Town in Wuding County, Yunnan Province, southern China. The single species, Wudingloong wui, is known from a partial articulated skeleton (LFGT-YW002) preserving most of the skull, the anterior axial column, and a complete right forelimb. Wang et al. (2025) recover Wudingloong as sister to Plateosauravus + Ruehleia, outside Massospondylidae and Sauropodiformes, and argue it is both the earliest-diverging and stratigraphically oldest sauropodomorph known from East Asia.
diagnostic_features: Ascending ramus of the maxilla excavated by a triangular antorbital fossa.
Axial intercentrum completely fused to the axis and slightly mediolaterally wider than the anterior surface of the axial centrum.
Distinct blade-like ventral keel on the middle cervical centra, extending the full length of the centrum.
Humerus with a slender shaft (minimum width 0.12x total length) and a flat, low, only slightly convex humeral head.
Ungual of manual digit I large and robust, with length ~2.9x and proximal height and width ~3.2x those of the ungual of manual digit III.
Metacarpal V gracile with an hourglass-shaped outline; proximal end approximately as wide transversely as the distal end.

Wyleyia.etymology: Named in honor of J. F. Wyley, who discovered the specimen in Weald Clay deposits of Henfield, Sussex, England.
Wyleyia.description: Wyleyia is an extinct genus of indeterminate maniraptoran dinosaurs containing a single species, Wyleyia valdensis, known from the early Cretaceous period of Sussex, England. The genus is known from a single specimen, a damaged right humerus. It was named to honor J. F. Wyley, who found the specimen in Weald Clay deposits of Henfield in Sussex (England). The specific name valdensis means "from the Weald".

Xenoceratops.etymology: From Greek 'xenos' meaning 'foreign' or 'alien' and 'ceratops' meaning 'horned face', referring to the scarcity of ceratopsian species known from the Foremost Formation.
Xenoceratops.description: Xenoceratops is a genus of centrosaurine ceratopsid dinosaur known from the Late Cretaceous (middle Campanian stage), and is known to have lived in what is currently Alberta, Canada. The genus has one known species, Xenoceratops foremostensis, after its place of discovery, the Foremost Formation.

Xenoposeidon.etymology: From Greek xenos meaning 'strange' or 'alien' and Poseidon (the Greek god of the sea), in allusion to the sauropod genus Sauroposeidon; translates as 'strange Poseidon'
Xenoposeidon.description: Xenoposeidon is a genus of rebbachisaurid sauropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of England, living about 140 million years ago. It is known from a single partial vertebra with unusual features, unlike those of other sauropods. This bone was first discovered in the early 1890s but received little attention until it was found by University of Portsmouth student Mike Taylor, who formally described and named it in 2007 with Darren Naish.

Accessory infraparapophyseal and postzygapophyseal laminae meeting ventrally to form a V
Neural canal is asymmetric: small and circular posteriorly but tall and teardrop-shaped anteriorly
Supporting laminae form vaulted arch over anterior neural canal

Xenovenator.etymology: From Greek xenos ('strange') and Latin venator ('hunter'), meaning 'strange hunter'
Xenovenator.description: Xenovenator is an extinct genus of troodontid theropod dinosaurs known from the Late Cretaceous (Campanian age) of North America. The type species of the genus, Xenovenator espinosai, is known from fragmentary skull bones found in the Cerro del Pueblo Formation of Mexico. It is characterized by an unusually expanded and rugose skull roof, somewhat comparable to that seen in pachycephalosaurs. This may imply Xenovenator individuals engaged in combat with other members of their species, a behavior for which adaptations had not been previously observed in non-avian paravians.
diagnostic_features: Frontals extensively fused with strongly interdigitating sutures
Strong doming of frontals projecting above orbital margins
Frontals and parietals massively thickened (up to 12 mm posteriorly) with variable thickness
Dorsal surface of frontals and parietals rugose and striated with transverse ridge texture
Nasal processes broad and transversely arched between lacrimals forming broad midline ridge
Orbital fossae widely separated ventrally with orbital margins expanded laterally
Triangular parietal table just behind frontoparietal suture, not seen in other troodontids
Laterosphenoids and orbitosphenoids strongly expanded anteriorly to enclose braincase ventrally
Supratemporal fossae extend strongly anterolaterally with frontoparietal suture projecting posteriorly
L-shaped frontal-lacrimal contact with complex posterior and medial facets

Xiangyunloong.etymology: From Chinese 'Xiangyun' (auspicious clouds), the name of the county where the specimen was found, and 'loong', the Pinyin for the traditional Chinese dragon symbolizing power and auspiciousness.
Xiangyunloong.description: Xiangyunloong is a genus of non-sauropodan massopodan sauropodomorph dinosaur known from the Early Jurassic Fengjiahe Formation at Daaonai, Xiangyun County, Yunnan Province, China. The genus contains a single species, Xiangyunloong fengming, known from a partial postcranial skeleton of a skeletally mature individual estimated at about 9–10 m in length.

Hyposphene of dorsal vertebrae equal to or greater than the height of the neural canal.
Highly developed posterodorsal corner present at the neural spine of the last dorsal vertebra.
Presence of a prezygapophyseal centrodiapophyseal fossa (PRCDF) in the first caudal vertebra, framed by ACDL, CPRL, and PRDL laminae.
Ilium with anteroposteriorly reduced but laterally and ventrally flaring supracetabular crest.

holotype.material: Partial skeleton: three cervical, five dorsal, and fifteen caudal vertebrae; several dorsal rib fragments; nearly a dozen chevrons; an incomplete left ilium; and a right ischium.

Xianshanosaurus.etymology: Named after Xianshan Hill near the fossil locality in the Ruyang Basin, Henan Province, China, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Xianshanosaurus.description: Xianshanosaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous (Aptian-Albian) of the Ruyang Basin in Henan Province, China. Its type and only species is Xianshanosaurus shijiagouensis. It was described in 2009 by a team of paleontologists led by Lü Junchang. Xianshanosaurus may be a titanosaur, and Daxiatitan may be its closest relative, but its evolutionary relationships remain controversial.

Neural spines of anterior caudal vertebrae plate-like with coarse areas on the middle portions of the anterior and posterior surfaces.
Distinct fossae present on the anterolateral surface of the base of the prezygapophysis and the anterior surface of the base of the transverse process.
Coracoid foramen located closely to the scapula-coracoid suture.
Shallow concavity present on the proximal end of the dorsal ribs.

Xiaotingia.description: Xiaotingia is a genus of paravian theropod dinosaur, possibly an anchiornithid, from Middle Jurassic or early Late Jurassic deposits of western Liaoning, China. It contains a single species, Xiaotingia zhengi.

Xingtianosaurus.description: Xingtianosaurus is an extinct genus of oviraptorosaurian theropod dinosaur that lived in what is now China during the Early Cretaceous. The type and only species, X. ganqi, was named and described in 2019. It was placed in the Caudipteridae, alongside Caudipteryx and Similicaudipteryx.

Extremely short metacarpal I less than 40% the length of metacarpal II
Small ligament pits on the manual phalanges, dorsally located

Xingxiulong.etymology: Named for the Xingxiu Bridge (Xingxiu meaning 'constellation' in Chinese) in Yunnan, China, combined with Chinese 'long' meaning 'dragon'.
Xingxiulong.description: Xingxiulong is a genus of bipedal massopodan sauropodomorph from the Early Jurassic of China. It contains two species; the type species is X. chengi, described by Wang et al. in 2017 from three specimens, two adults and an immature individual, that collectively constitute a mostly complete skeleton. Adults of this species measured 4-5 meters (13-16 ft) long and 1-1.5 meters (3.3-4.9 ft) tall. A second species, X. yueorum, was described by Chen et al. in 2025 based on a partial articulated postcranial skeleton of an adult individual larger than X. chengi.

posterolateral process of distal tibia much narrower and extended more laterally and distally than anterolateral process
metatarsal V with markedly expanded proximal end approximately 85% of total length
angular and surangular extended more anteriorly beyond external mandibular fenestra

Xinjiangovenator.etymology: Named after Xinjiang, the autonomous region of China where it was found, combined with Latin venator meaning 'hunter'; translates as 'Xinjiang hunter'
Xinjiangovenator.description: Xinjiangovenator is a genus of coelurosaurian dinosaurs, possibly part of the group Maniraptora, which lived in the Lianmuqin Formation of the Tugulu Group of China, dated to the Early Cretaceous period, sometime between the Valanginian and Albian stages.

Fibular condyle of tibia extending posteriorly beyond lateral side of proximal tibia, separated by step rather than notch
Ascending process of astragalus arising from complete breadth of astragalar body and very high (approximately three times height of astragalar body)
Small theropod with tibia plus proximal tarsals length of 312 mm

Xinjiangtitan.etymology: From Xinjiang, the autonomous region of northwestern China where it was found, and titan ('giant'), meaning 'Xinjiang titan'
Xinjiangtitan.description: Xinjiangtitan is an extinct genus of mamenchisaurid sauropod that lived during the Middle Jurassic of what is now Xinjiang, northwestern China. Its type and only species is Xinjiangtitan shanshanesis (Chinese: 鄯善新疆巨龙; pinyin: Shànshàn Xīnjiāngjùlóng), known from a single incomplete skeleton recovered from the Qiketai Formation. The holotype preserves one of the most complete vertebral columns of any sauropod found in Asia, and has the longest complete neck known for any animal.
diagnostic_features: Ventral keel developed at posterior 1/4 of penultimate cervical centrum, forming small semicircular projection under distal articular facet
Last two cervical vertebrae very elongated (sum of lengths is 63% of combined femur and tibia length)
First dorsal rib does not participate in forming sternal plate
Femur very robust with maximum distal width 33% of femoral length
Four dorsal vertebrae present (opisthocoelous and not fused to one another)
First and second sacral ribs simultaneously connected to second sacral rib, with first sacral rib not participating in sacrocostal yoke
Pubis very flat with well-developed ambiens process extending distally
Fourth trochanter located on posteromedial edge of femur

Xiongguanlong.etymology: From Chinese 'Xiong Guan' meaning 'grand pass', referring to Jiayuguan City (historically called Xiong Guan), and Chinese 'long' meaning 'dragon'.
Xiongguanlong.description: Xiongguanlong is an extinct genus of tyrannosauroid theropod from the Early Cretaceous period of what is now China. The type and only species is X. baimoensis. The generic name comes from Jiayuguan City (formerly called "Xiong Guan" or "grand pass") and the Mandarin word "long" which means dragon. The specific epithet, "baimoensis" is a latinization of the Mandarin word for "white ghost" in reference to one of the geological features of the type locality (nicknamed the "White Ghost Castle").

Narrow and elongate muzzle resembling that of Alioramus
Slender, unornamented nasals lacking dorsal rugosities and vaulting
Narrow and mediolaterally compressed maxillary tooth crowns bearing serrations
Single pair of pneumatic foramina on each cervical (unlike double pairs in derived taxa)
Mediolaterally constricted anterior dorsal centra

distal tarsals and metatarsals co-ossified to form tarsometatarsus

Xixiasaurus.etymology: Named for Xixia County, Henan Province, China, where the holotype was discovered, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard', translatable as 'Henan Xixia lizard'.
Xixiasaurus.description: Xixiasaurus is a genus of troodontid dinosaur that lived during the Late Cretaceous Period in what is now China. The only known specimen was discovered in Xixia County, Henan Province, in central China, and became the holotype of the new genus and species Xixiasaurus henanensis in 2010. The names refer to the areas of discovery, and can be translated as "Henan Xixia lizard". The specimen consists of an almost complete skull (except for the hindmost portion), part of the lower jaw, and teeth, as well as a partial right forelimb.
diagnostic_features: Fewer maxillary teeth (22) than Byronosaurus (>30) and Mei (24)
Distinct opening on the lateral surface of the base of the nasal process of the premaxilla
Rostral end of the upper jaw forming a tapered U-shape in ventral view
Mandibular symphyseal region slightly inflected medially
Unserrated teeth on anterior and posterior carinae, unlike most other troodontids

Xuanhanosaurus.etymology: Named for Xuanhan County in Sichuan, China, where the fossils were recovered, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Xuanhanosaurus.description: Xuanhanosaurus is a genus of theropod dinosaur that lived during the Middle Jurassic (Bathonian) of the Sichuan Basin, China, around 166 million years ago. This taxon represents one of the various non-coelurosaurian tetanuran taxa found on the Middle Jurassic of the region, uncovered in the Lower Shaximiao Formation. Although it has been known for more than 40 years, this taxon has been the subject of very few studies, although most seem to agree that it is a tetanuran, possibly a basal allosauroid, highlighting the fact that it has a vestigial fourth metacarpal.
diagnostic_features: Forelimbs relatively well developed with fourth metacarpal retained (primitive characteristic within Megalosauridae)
Forelimbs possess ambulatory function, contrasting with later-stage tyrannosaurids
Well-developed ventral crest on cervical vertebrae, wing-shaped and prominent
Tridactyl manus with stout, short, non-strongly-curved claws
Cervical vertebrae with posterior concavity and undeveloped anterior projection

Xuanhuaceratops.description: Xuanhuaceratops is a genus of dinosaur from the Late Jurassic Period. The genus was in 2006 dated to the Tithonian, 150.8-145.5 million years ago. A member of the family Chaoyangsauridae, it was one of the earliest ceratopsians. The fossils were found in the Houcheng Formation of Hebei Province, northeastern China.

Xunmenglong.etymology: From Chinese xun ('swift'), meng ('fierce'), and long ('dragon'), meaning 'swift fierce dragon'
Xunmenglong.description: Xunmenglong is a genus of compsognathid theropod dinosaur from the Huajiying Formation of Hebei Province, China. The type and only species is Xunmenglong yinliangis. The holotype material consists of a pelvis, tail base and hindlimbs that had previously been part of a chimera containing three different animals. The animal is described as being the smallest known member of Compsognathidae, being about the size of the sub-adult Scipionyx holotype specimen, or approximately 50 centimeters (1.6 ft) in length.

Ilium with straight dorsal outline and rounded anterior margin in lateral view

Three ossified distal tarsals II, III, and IV

Xuwulong.etymology: Named after pioneering Gansu Province geologist Wang Yue-lun, known by his courtesy name 'Xu-wu', combined with Chinese 'long' meaning 'dragon'
Xuwulong.description: Xuwulong is a genus of hadrosauroid dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous period of what is now Yujingzi Basin in the Jiuquan area, Gansu Province of northwestern China. It is known from the holotype, GSGM F00001, an articulated specimen including a complete cranium, almost complete axial skeleton, and complete left pelvic girdle recovered from the Xinminbao Group. Xuwulong was named by You Hailu, Li Daqing, and Liu Weichang in 2011, and the type species is Xuwulong yueluni; the binomial name as a whole refers to Professor Wang Yue-lun; "Xu-wu" is his courtesy name.

Yamanasaurus.etymology: Named after the locality of Yamana in southern Ecuador where the fossils were found, combined with Greek sauros meaning 'lizard'; translates as 'Yamana lizard'
Yamanasaurus.description: Yamanasaurus is an extinct genus of saltasaurine titanosaurian dinosaur from the Río Playas Formation of Ecuador, which dates to the Campanian-Maastrichtian of the late Cretaceous period (approximately 75-70 million years ago). The type and only species is Yamanasaurus lojaensis, representing the first non-avian dinosaur described from Ecuador. The holotype, consisting of fragments of a humerus, ulna, tibia, two sacral vertebrae and a single caudal, was discovered in 2017.

Radius robust with flattened diaphysis and marked neck under epiphysis with heptagonal proximal articular surface

Yanbeilong.description: Yanbeilong is an extinct genus of stegosaurian dinosaurs from the Early Cretaceous (Albian age) Zuoyun Formation of Shanxi, China. The genus contains a single species, Yanbeilong ultimus, known from a single partial skeleton including several vertebrae and the pelvic girdle. It is one of the youngest known stegosaurs, alongside Mongolostegus from Mongolia and unnamed stegosaurine remains from the Hekou Group of China, both of which date to the Aptian-Albian ages.

Yangchuanosaurus.etymology: Named for Yongchuan (historically romanized as Yangchuan), the district in Sichuan Province, China, where the fossils were found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Yangchuanosaurus.description: Yangchuanosaurus is an extinct genus of metriacanthosaurid theropod dinosaur that lived in China from the Middle Jurassic to Late Jurassic periods (Bathonian to Tithonian stages), and was similar (although slightly larger) in size and appearance to its North American and European relative, Allosaurus. Yangchuanosaurus hails from the Upper Shaximiao Formation and was the largest predator in a landscape that included the sauropods Mamenchisaurus and Omeisaurus and the stegosaurs Chialingosaurus, Tuojiangosaurus and Chungkingosaurus. This theropod was named after the area in which was discovered, Yongchuan, in China.

Pubis fused to distal end of ischium; pubic foot poorly developed; ascending process of astragalus poorly formed

Yantaloong.etymology: From Chinese 'Yanta' (wild goose tower, a noted historical site in the Chuxiong Yi Autonomous Prefecture where the holotype was collected) and Mandarin 'loong' (dragon).
Yantaloong.description: Yantaloong is an extinct genus of basal eusauropod dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic middle Zhanghe Formation at Zhongbanjing Village, Yuanmou County, Chuxiong Yi Autonomous Prefecture, Yunnan Province, China. The single species, Yantaloong lini, is known from six nearly complete presacral vertebrae of an adult individual. Phylogenetic analyses by Zhang et al. (2026) recover Yantaloong as an early-branching member of an expanded Turiasauria, in a clade with Lapparentosaurus, Atlasaurus, and Jobaria, sister to the 'traditional' Iberian / North American turiasaurians. The authors claim Yantaloong is the first turiasaurian sauropod known from East Asia and argue its presence undermines the hypothesized East Asian sauropodomorph isolation. The expanded Turiasauria definition is single-paper-recent; the conservative parent Eusauropoda is used here pending broader adoption.
diagnostic_features: Posterior-most cervical vertebra bears a bifurcated posterior centrodiapophyseal lamina (bif.PCDL) and a bifurcated centropostzygapophyseal lamina (bif.CPOL).
Anterior-most dorsal vertebra has both an upper and a lower anterior centroparapophyseal lamina (u.ACPL and l.ACPL), with a small fossa at the anteroventral corner of the parapophysis.

Middle dorsal vertebrae bear a lamina-like anteromedial centropostzygapophyseal lamina (am.CPOL) and a prezygoparapophyseal lamina (PRPL) bifurcated both dorsally and ventrally with a ventral PRPL fossa.
Middle dorsal vertebrae possess a rhombus-shaped hyposphene supported by a vertical ventral infrahyposphenal lamina and paired ventrolateral infrahyposphenal laminae.
Posterior dorsal neural arches bear a dorsoventrally elongated oval-shaped hyposphene.

Yehuecauhceratops.etymology: From Nahuatl yehuecauh meaning 'ancient' combined with Greek keras meaning 'horn' and ops meaning 'face'; translates as 'ancient horned face'
Yehuecauhceratops.description: Yehuecauhceratops is a genus of horned centrosaurine ceratopsid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Coahuila, Mexico. It contains a single species, Y. mudei, described from two partial specimens by Rivera-Sylva et al. in 2016 and formally named by Rivera-Sylva et al. in 2017. It was a small centrosaurine with a body length of 3 meters (9.8 ft), making it smaller than Agujaceratops and Coahuilaceratops, the other two ceratopsids in its environment; the three may have been ecologically segregated. A ridge bearing a single roughened projection near the bottom of the squamosal bone, which probably supported a small horn, allows Yehuecauhceratops to be distinguished from other centrosaurines. Its affinities to nasutoceratopsin centrosaurines, such as Avaceratops and Nasutoceratops, are supported by various morphological similarities to the former.

Yeneen.etymology: Named after Yeneen, an entity in Tehuelche (Aonikenk) culture tied to cold and winter weather; references the type locality La Invernada, a Spanish word for the wintering location of cattle.
Yeneen.description: Yeneen is an extinct genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaurs known from the Late Cretaceous (Santonian age) Bajo de la Carpa Formation of Argentina. The genus contains a single species, Yeneen houssayi, known from at least one partial skeleton. Its discovery highlights the diversity of titanosaurs in this formation, which also includes Bonitasaura, Inawentu, Overosaurus, Rinconsaurus, and Traukutitan.

Yimenosaurus.etymology: Named after Yimen County (also written as Yiman) in Yunnan Province, China where it was found, combined with Greek sauros meaning 'lizard'; translates as 'Yiman reptile'
Yimenosaurus.description: Yimenosaurus is an extinct genus of plateosaurid sauropodomorph dinosaur that lived in China in the Early Jurassic. The genus was first named in 1990 by Ziqi Bai, Jie Yang and Guohui Wang, along with its type and only species, Yimenosaurus youngi. The species name honors renowned Chinese paleontologist Yang Zhongjian, the father of Chinese paleontology, known as C.C. Young in English. Known material includes the holotype, an almost complete skull and mandible, as well as incomplete cervical and dorsal vertebrae, a mostly complete sacrum, an ilium, ischia, partial ribs and complete femur, and a paratype, a well-preserved postcrania with a fragmentary skull. In 2010 Paul estimated its length at 9 meters (30 ft) and its weight at 2 tonnes (2.2 short tons).
diagnostic_features: Moderate to large prosauropod attaining nine meters in length with relatively delicate skull
Cranial construction with relatively long and gracile elements composing the skull
Elliptical external nares and large triangular antorbital fenestra

Mandible relatively delicately constructed with well-developed mandibular fenestra positioned higher than in Lufengosaurus and Plateosaurus
Amphicoelous cervical and dorsal vertebrae with low neural arches and spines, lacking pleurocoels
Four premaxillary teeth, 17-18 maxillary teeth, 21-23 dentary teeth with compact arrangement
Teeth with relatively high spoon-shaped crowns with gently convex labial margin and conspicuous striations
Robust femur with conspicuous sinuous curvature and well-developed fourth trochanter located posterodorsally on midshaft
Short humerus three-fifths femur length, thick, lacking curvature with well-developed medial head

Yingshanosaurus.etymology: Named after Yingshan (a locality in Sichuan Province, China), combined with Greek sauros meaning 'lizard'; translates as 'Yingshan lizard'
Yingshanosaurus.description: Yingshanosaurus is an extinct genus of stegosaurian dinosaurs from the Middle Jurassic of what is now Southwestern China. It is known from a partial skeleton discovered in 1983, including back, sacrum, and tail vertebrae, forelimb and hindlimb bones, shoulder and hip bones, and several osteoderms, including plates and a shoulder spine. The genus contains a single species, Yingshanosaurus jichuanensis, named and described in 1994. For some time after its discovery and scientific description, many paleontologists were unaware of the Chinese research published on it and questioned its validity.

Reinforced pelvic girdle with deep acetabulum and prominent pubic tubercle

Yizhousaurus.etymology: Named for the Yizhou region (Chuxiong Yi Autonomous Region) of Yunnan, China, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Yizhousaurus.description: Yizhousaurus is a genus of basal sauropodiform dinosaurs which existed in what is now Lufeng Formation, Yunnan Province of southern China during the lower Jurassic period. Identified from a nearly complete and exquisitely preserved skeleton, it is the most complete basal sauropod currently known with intact skull. Although its name was revealed in a 2010 Geological Society of America abstract by Sankar Chatterjee, T. Wang, S.G. Pan, Z. Dong, X.C. Wu, and Paul Upchurch, it wasn't validly named and described until 2018. The type species is Yizhousaurus sunae.

Ypupiara.etymology: From Tupi (indigenous Brazilian language) meaning 'the one who lives in the water,' derived from a figure in Tupi mythology
Ypupiara.description: Ypupiara is an extinct genus of unenlagiine theropod from the Late Cretaceous Serra da Galga Formation of Brazil. It was the first member of the Dromaeosauridae to be discovered in South America and the first member of the Unenlagiinae to be discovered, but not the first to be identified as such. The type and only species, Y. lopai, is known solely from a specimen that was destroyed in a fire in 2018.

Rectangular and anteroposteriorly expanded interdental plate
Labiolingual compression of teeth with diameter >3/5 of rostrocaudal diameter

Absence of mesial and distal carinae on teeth
Fluted tooth surfaces with two or more longitudinal grooves

Yuanmouraptor.etymology: From 'Yuanmou' (Yuanmou County, Yunnan Province, China, the type locality) and Latin 'raptor' (robber).
Yuanmouraptor.description: Yuanmouraptor is an extinct genus of basal metriacanthosaurid theropod from the early Middle Jurassic (Aalenian-Bajocian) Zhanghe Formation at Xiabanjing Village, Yuanmou County, Chuxiong Yi Autonomous Prefecture, Yunnan Province, China. The single species, Yuanmouraptor jinshajiangensis, is known from a near-complete skull with mandible (reconstructed length ~60 cm) articulated with 10 cervical vertebrae and the first dorsal (LFGT-ZLJ0115). Zou et al. (2025) recover Yuanmouraptor as the most basal-branching member of Metriacanthosauridae in their equal-weights phylogenetic analysis.
diagnostic_features: Anterior process of postorbital sheet-shaped with depth remaining consistent throughout its length.
Ventral ramus of postorbital bearing a laterally twisted trough running along its lateral surface.
Strongly posteriorly elongated epipophyses on anterior cervical vertebrae.
Strongly ventromedially excavated pneumatic foramen on the third cervical vertebra.
Posterior cervical vertebrae with sheet-shaped and subrectangular neural spines.

Yuanmousaurus.etymology: Named for Yuanmou County in Yunnan, China, where the fossils were recovered, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Yuanmousaurus.description: Yuanmousaurus was a sauropod dinosaur from the Middle Jurassic period of China. It is known from incomplete remains, recovered in 2000 from the Zhanghe Formation in Yuanmou County in Yunnan Province. Yuanmousaurus was a relatively large sauropod and may have reached about 17 meters (56 ft) in length. It was a basal member of the Sauropoda, but its exact systematic position is unclear. A recent study placed Yuanmousaurus within the family Mamenchisauridae. It may be a dubious genus. The only and type species was Yuanmousaurus jiangyiensis.

Deltopectoral crest narrow, ratio of humeral length to femoral length approximately 0.72
Fourth trochanter is low and rounded

Yuanyanglong.description: Yuanyanglong is an extinct genus of oviraptorosaurian theropod dinosaurs from the Early Cretaceous Miaogou Formation of China. The genus contains a single species, Yuanyanglong bainian, known from two partial skeletons.

Yunmenglong.etymology: Named after the Yunmengshan area of Henan Province, China where it was found, combined with Chinese long meaning 'dragon'; translates as 'Yunmeng dragon'
Yunmenglong.description: Yunmenglong is an extinct genus of somphospondylan sauropod known from the late Early Cretaceous of Henan Province, central China. Its remains were discovered in the Haoling Formation of the Ruyang Basin. The type species is Yunmenglong ruyangensis, described in 2013 by Junchang Lü et al. on the basis of an incomplete postcranial skeleton. Yunmenglong shares some characters with Euhelopus, Qiaowanlong, and Erketu; a phylogenetic analysis places it as a sister taxon of Qiaowanlong, both grouped with Erketu in a position more derived than Euhelopus but basal to Titanosauria.

Two fossae on longitudinal depression of lateral surfaces of cervicals: anterior shallow and posterior deep piercing centrum

Yunnanosaurus.description: Yunnanosaurus is an extinct genus of sauropodomorph dinosaur that lived approximately 199 to 183 million years ago in what is now the Yunnan Province, in China, for which it was named. Yunnanosaurus was a large sized, moderately-built, ground-dwelling, quadrupedal herbivore, that could also walk bipedally, and ranged in size from 7 meters (23 feet) long and 2 m (6.5 ft) high to 4 m (13 ft) high in the largest species.

Zalmoxes.etymology: Named after Zalmoxis (also spelled Zamolxis), a deity or legendary king worshipped by the Getae people of ancient Thrace and Dacia (modern Romania), where the fossil was found.
Zalmoxes.description: Zalmoxes is a genus of probable rhabdodontid ornithopod dinosaur from the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous in what is now Romania. The genus is known from specimens first named as the species Mochlodon robustum in 1899 by Franz Nopcsa before being reclassified as Rhabdodon robustum by him in 1915. In 1990, this name was corrected to Rhabdodon robustus by George Olshevsky and, in 2003, the species was once more reclassified as the type species Zalmoxes robustus. Zalmoxes represents one of the most common vertebrates of Transylvania during the latest Cretaceous period. The generic name refers to the Dacian deity Zalmoxis and the specific name robustus refers to the robustness of the remains. Another species, Zalmoxes shqiperorum, was named in 2003, but this species has since been reassigned to a separate genus of ceratopsian, Ferenceratops.

Zavacephale.etymology: From Greek zava meaning 'origin' or 'beginning' and kephale meaning 'head'; translates as 'origin head,' referring to its status as the oldest known pachycephalosaur
Zavacephale.description: Zavacephale is an extinct genus of pachycephalosaurian dinosaurs known from the Early Cretaceous Khuren Dukh Formation of Mongolia. The genus contains a single species, Zavacephale rinpoche, known from a partial articulated skeleton including a nearly complete skull. It is both the oldest definitive pachycephalosaur known, as well as the most complete. Its skull bears a well-developed dome structure, as seen in most members of the clade.

Zhenyuanlong.etymology: Named after Sun Zhenyuan, who discovered the specimen, combined with Chinese Pinyin lóng (龙/龍) meaning 'dragon'; thus 'Zhenyuan's dragon'
Zhenyuanlong.description: Zhenyuanlong is a genus of dromaeosaurid dinosaur from the Yixian Formation of Liaoning, China. It lived during the Aptian age of the early Cretaceous period, approximately 125 million years ago. It is known from a single specimen belonging to the species Zhenyuanlong suni (Chinese: 孫氏振元龍). This type specimen preserved a nearly complete skeleton that contains traces of feathers, including long tail feathers and large wings. In addition to further complicating diversity of Liaoning dromaeosaurids, this specimen provides the first direct evidence of well-developed pennaceous feathers in a large, non-flying dromaeosaur, raising the question of what function such wings would serve.

Zhuchengceratops.etymology: Named for Zhucheng, the city in Shandong Province, China where the fossil was found, combined with Latinized Greek 'ceratops' meaning 'horned face'.
Zhuchengceratops.description: Zhuchengceratops is a genus of extinct leptoceratopsid ceratopsian that lived during the Upper Cretaceous of modern-day China. It was first described in 2010, by Xu et al., who created the binomial Zhuchengceratops inexpectus. The name is derived from the location of Zhucheng, the Latinized-Greek ceratops, or "horned face", and the unexpected articulated nature of the holotype. The skeleton was found in the Wangshi Group, which is of Late Cretaceous age, and most fossils are only disarticulated bones of Shantungosaurus.
diagnostic_features: Maxilla with posteroventrally oriented edentulous posterior process
Mandible extremely deep (mid-length height one-third of mandibular length) and very thin transversely
Medial surface of mandible with two large fossae separated by thick curved ridge along dentary-splenial contact
Predentary sub-vertically oriented (posterior edge ~75 degrees to tooth row in lateral view)
Anterior end of dentary deeper than coronoid region
Middle cervical ribs bifurcated with prominent accessory dorsal process

species.name: Zhuchengceratops inexpectus
species.etymology: From Latin 'inexpectus' meaning 'unexpected', referring to the surprising discovery of the articulated skeleton amid the otherwise largely disarticulated Zhucheng dinosaur assemblage.

holotype.material: Partial, articulated skeleton including partial maxillae, partial quadratojugal, jugal, quadrate, ectopterygoid, pterygoid, nearly complete mandibles, anterior 14 presacral vertebrae with ribs, and fragments

Zhuchengtitan.etymology: Named after Zhucheng, Shandong Province, China where it was found, combined with Greek titan meaning 'giant'; translates as 'Zhucheng titan'
Zhuchengtitan.description: Zhuchengtitan is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Shandong, China. It contains a single species, Z. zangjiazhuangensis, named by Mo Jinyou and colleagues in 2017 from a single humerus. Zhuchengtitan can be identified by the extreme width of the top end of its humerus, as well as the expansion of the deltopectoral crest on its humerus; both of these characteristics indicate that it was likely closely related to Opisthocoelicaudia. However, it differs from the latter by the flatter bottom articulating surface of its humerus. Zhuchengtitan lived in a floodplain environment alongside Shantungosaurus, Zhuchengtyrannus, and Sinoceratops.
diagnostic_features: Proximal portion strongly expanded transversely, maximum width reaching 55% of shaft length
Humeral shaft extremely robust with robustness index (RI) of 0.39
Deltopectoral crest expands distally and deflects medially to reach 2/5 of bone length
Prominent lateral convexity on outer proximal one-third of lateral margin
Mid-shaft cross-section elliptical with long axis oriented mediolaterally

species.etymology: Named for the Zangjiazhuang Quarry in Zhucheng, Shandong, China, where the holotype humerus was recovered.

Zhuchengtyrannus.etymology: Named after Zhucheng, Shandong Province, China (the type locality), combined with Latin tyrannus meaning 'tyrant'; translates as 'Zhucheng tyrant'
Zhuchengtyrannus.description: Zhuchengtyrannus is a genus of tyrannosaurid theropod dinosaur from Asia, known from the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous of Shandong Province, China. It belongs to the subfamily Tyrannosaurinae, and contains a single species, Zhuchengtyrannus magnus.
diagnostic_features: Horizontal shelf on lateral surface of base of ascending process of maxilla
Rounded notch in anterior margin of maxillary fenestra
Ventral margin of antorbital fenestra lies well above ventral rim of antorbital fossa
Anteroposterior length of maxillary fenestra more than half the distance between anterior margins of antorbital fossa and fenestra
Absence of subcutaneous flange on posterodorsal part of jugal ramus of maxilla
Absence of ventrally convex palatal shelf covering roots of posterior teeth in medial view

species.name: Zhuchengtyrannus magnus
species.etymology: From Latin 'magnus' meaning 'great', referring to the relatively large size of Zhuchengtyrannus among tyrannosaurids.

holotype.material: Nearly complete right maxilla and associated left dentary, both with teeth in situ

Ziapelta.etymology: Named after the Zia sun symbol, the stylized sun emblem of the Zia Pueblo people of New Mexico, where the fossil was found, combined with Greek 'pelta' meaning 'small shield', referring to its ankylosaur armor.
Ziapelta.description: Ziapelta is an extinct genus of ankylosaurid. Its fossils have been found in the Hunter Wash and De-na-zin members of the Kirtland Formation of Upper Cretaceous (Campanian) New Mexico. It was named in 2014, in a research paper led by ankylosaur researcher Victoria Arbour. There is a single species in the genus, Ziapelta sanjuanensis. The genus is named after the Zia sun symbol, a stylized sun with four groups of rays, having religious significance to the Zia people of New Mexico, and the iconic symbol on the state flag of New Mexico, and pelta (Latin), a small shield, in reference to the osteoderms found on all ankylosaurids. The specific name is in reference to San Juan County and the San Juan basin, where the fossils were found. Multiple specimens have been described to date, though the fossils are mostly from the front part of the animal. Its closest relative appears to be either Scolosaurus or Nodocephalosaurus, depending on what cladistic model is used.
diagnostic_features: Prominent, large, sub-triangular median nasal caputegulum
Dorsoventrally deep squamosal horns curved anteriorly at the tips
Three deep fossae on the ventral surface of the basicranium
Mixture of flat and weakly bulbous frontonasal caputegulae

species.name: Ziapelta sanjuanensis
species.etymology: Named for San Juan County and the San Juan Basin in New Mexico, USA, where the fossils were discovered.

holotype.institution: New Mexico Museum of Natural History and Science
holotype.material: Complete skull, left side of first cervical half ring, fragmentary second cervical half ring, and numerous fragmentary postcranial osteoderms

Zigongosaurus.etymology: Named for Zigong City in Sichuan, China, where the fossils were found, combined with Greek 'sauros' meaning 'lizard'.
Zigongosaurus.description: Zigongosaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur from the Middle-Late Jurassic-aged Shaximiao Formation of Zigong, Sichuan, China. Because of incomplete knowledge of Jurassic Chinese sauropods, it has been hard to interpret, with some sources assigning it to Omeisaurus, some to Mamenchisaurus, and some to its own genus.
diagnostic_features: Anterior edge of the maxilla above the tooth row bears a forward-and-downward projecting process contacting the premaxillary suture; maxillary foramen not prominent
Maxilla bearing 12-14 teeth and mandible 15-17 teeth
Prefrontal forming the main component of the dorsal orbital border; posterior part of the temporal bone exceptionally thick (up to 18 mm); upper temporal fenestra oval and narrow anteroposteriorly

Premaxillary teeth largest, with long pointed crowns bearing small apical tubercles but no serrations; cheek-tooth crowns convex externally and concave internally with a prominent internal median ridge
Anterior end of the dentary symphysis projecting downward with a rough external surface; lower margin of the dentary bearing a longitudinal groove extending to the symphysis

Zizhongosaurus.etymology: Named after Zizhong County in Sichuan Province, China where it was found, combined with Greek sauros meaning 'lizard'; translates as 'Zizhong lizard'
Zizhongosaurus.description: Zizhongosaurus is a genus of basal herbivorous sauropod dinosaur which lived in the Early Jurassic (Toarcian) Period of China. It was a large-bodied herbivore characterized by a long neck.
diagnostic_features: Small primitive sauropod with relatively long anterior limbs
Humerus with straight and rounded shaft
Dorsal vertebrae with high neural spine with apex as expanded plate descending slightly anteriorly and concave posteriorly
Lateral spine surface ornamented with dorsally radiating vertical striations
Well-developed diapophyses forming right angle with neural spine at neural arch
Hyposphene present

Zuniceratops.etymology: From Zuni, referring to the Zuni people of New Mexico near where the specimen was found, and Greek keratops meaning 'horned face'; thus 'Zuni horned face'
Zuniceratops.description: Zuniceratops is a genus of ceratopsian dinosaurs that lived during the Turonian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now New Mexico, United States. Only a single species is known, Zuniceratops christopheri.

Decurved ischium more curved than Centrosaurus but less than Triceratops
Gracile appendicular skeleton resembling protoceratopsids
Caudal extension of tooth row on maxilla beyond ascending process

Zuolong.etymology: Named in honor of General Zuo Zongtang (also known as General Tso), a 19th-century Chinese military leader, combined with Chinese 'long' meaning 'dragon'.
Zuolong.description: Zuolong is an extinct genus of tetanuran theropod from the Late Jurassic period of China. The type and only species is Z. salleei. The generic name of Zuolong is in honor of General Zuo Zōngtáng (also known as "General Tso") with the Chinese word "long" which means dragon. The specific epithet "salleei" is in honor of Hilmar Sallee, who funded the expedition which led to the specimen's discovery.
diagnostic_features: Large slit-like quadrate foramen inclined medially at ~45° with associated deep fossa on the quadrate
Sacral centrum 5 with obliquely oriented posterior articular surface angled anterodorsally
Fovea capitis very large, occupying almost entire posterodorsal surface of femoral head
Distal condyle of metatarsal III large with anteromedially projecting flange

Zuoyunlong.description: Zuoyunlong is an extinct genus of herbivorous ornithopod dinosaur belonging to the Hadrosauroidea that lived during the Late Cretaceous in the area of present China.

Zupaysaurus.etymology: From Quechua supay meaning 'devil' and Greek sauros (σαυρος) meaning 'lizard'; thus 'devil lizard'
Zupaysaurus.description: Zupaysaurus is an extinct genus of early theropod dinosaur living during the Norian stage of the Late Triassic in what is now Argentina. Fossils of the dinosaur were found in the Los Colorados Formation of the Ischigualasto-Villa Unión Basin in northwestern Argentina. Although a full skeleton has not yet been discovered, Zupaysaurus can be considered a bipedal predator, up to 4 meters (13 ft) long. It may have had two parallel crests running the length of its snout.
diagnostic_features: Oval, anteroventrally oriented antorbital fenestra
Two parasagittal crests on snout formed by nasals
Maxilla with parallel dorsal and ventral borders (unlike most other theropods)
Tibial-astragalar articulation locked medioposteriorly by astragalar process in posteriorly open tibial notch
Transversely expanded distal end of tibia with wide postfibular wing
Tooth row ending anterior to orbit (tetanuran trait)

Zuul.etymology: Named after Zuul, the fictional monster from the 1984 film Ghostbusters, due to the resemblance of its skull to the creature's face
Zuul.description: Zuul is a genus of herbivorous ankylosaurine dinosaur from the Campanian Judith River Formation of Montana. The type species is Zuul crurivastator. It is known from a complete skull and tail, which represents the first ankylosaurin known from a complete skull and tail club, as well as the most complete ankylosaurid specimen thus far recovered from North America. The specimen also preserved in situ osteoderms, keratin, and skin remains.
diagnostic_features: Frontonasal and frontoparietal caputegulae imbricated with distinct posteriorly located peaked apices.
Prefrontal, frontoparietal, and middle supraorbital caputegulae strongly pyramidal with small bases and tall peaks.
Squamosal horns with prominent longitudinal furrows on the lateral surface converging toward the apex.
Lateral caudal osteoderms along the tail club handle with strongly concave leading edges and posteriorly offset apices.
Tail club knob dorsoventrally flat with height-to-length ratio less than 0.20.

species.name: Zuul crurivastator
species.etymology: From Latin 'crus' meaning 'shank' and 'vastator' meaning 'destroyer', reading as 'Destroyer of Shins' in reference to the presumed defensive tactic of smashing the lower legs of predatory theropods with its tail club.

holotype.material: Nearly complete cranium, both lower jaws, disarticulated cervical vertebrae, articulated dorsal and sacral vertebrae, dorsal ribs, pelvic elements, complete articulated tail with tail club, in situ osteoderms, ossicles, and skin impressions.
